### Finding 146 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, low-moderate - `vault-quick-fix-actions.ts`'s own local `requireCompanyId(companyId)` was the one hyphenated-`*-actions.ts` holdout the 2026-11-06 `requireCompanyId()` sweep (`b002f4e`) never reached, because its signature differs from every other copy's)

**Area:** Tender Workspace "Quick Blocker Resolver" drawer
(`app/app/tenders/[id]/vault-quick-fix-actions.ts`, called from
`quick-blocker-drawer.tsx`'s `saveVaultQuickFields()`/`uploadCoidQuickFix()`).

**Scenario:** the standing backlog named the 33-hyphenated-`*-actions.ts`-file
surface as "flagged as a remaining surface, not yet re-visited" since the
2026-11-06 passes that (a) swept `requireCompanyId()`'s own `company_members`
read for a missing `error` capture across 23 Server Action files (`b002f4e`)
and (b) re-checked the "actions.ts out of scope" exclusion a second time
(finding `requireCompanyId()` itself was the exact bug, not a different
class). Checked `git log -1` recency across every currently-existing
hyphenated `*-actions.ts` file (12 total, not 33 - the number has shrunk as
earlier sweeps folded some in) rather than trusting the backlog's framing:
10 of the 12 were last touched in the 2026-11-06 sweeps themselves;
`update-actions.ts` (2026-10-20, read in full, already captures its one RPC
call's error correctly - no finding) and `vault-quick-fix-actions.ts`
(2026-10-24, pre-dating every 2026-11-06 fix) were the two genuinely
untouched since. `vault-quick-fix-actions.ts`'s own `requireCompanyId()`
turned out to be a real, if narrow, miss: unlike every one of the 23 swept
files (`.eq("user_id", user.id).maybeSingle()`, no caller-supplied company
id), this file's own copy additionally takes a client-passed `companyId`
argument and cross-checks it (`.eq("user_id", ...).eq("company_id",
companyId).maybeSingle()`) - a real, correctly-designed tenant-isolation
check (the drawer is a client component calling a Server Action with a
`companyId` prop, so this is the actual defense against a mismatched or
spoofed id, not dead code). That different signature is almost certainly why
`b002f4e`'s own sweep (grepping for the common single-argument shape) never
matched it, and it still discarded the read's own `error` entirely.

**Consequence, traced to its real severity rather than assumed:** this does
NOT fail open - a transient `company_members` read failure still fell
through to `membership` being `undefined`/falsy, so both callers
(`saveVaultQuickFields()`, `uploadCoidQuickFix()`) correctly denied the write
either way. The actual bug is the same "swallowed Supabase error" shape this
whole review has tracked, just resolving to a misleading DENIAL instead of a
false grant: a legitimately-signed-in member of the company, hit by a
transient read failure while using the drawer, was told "Not signed in to
this company." - the exact same non-actionable, wrong-reason message the
23-file sweep replaced with "Couldn't verify your company - try again."
everywhere else in this codebase. No data loss, no cross-tenant write, no
security gap - a reliability/UX inconsistency, left exactly where the sweep
that fixed every sibling never looked.

**Fix:** `requireCompanyId()` now captures `membershipError`, logs it
(`console.error`), and returns a discriminated `{ ok: true; companyId } |
{ ok: false; error }` result instead of `string | null`, so the two denial
reasons are distinguishable - genuinely-not-a-member still gets "Not signed
in to this company.", a real read failure now gets "Couldn't verify your
company - try again." (matching the sibling convention exactly). Both
callers updated to read `verified.ok`/`verified.error`/`verified.companyId`
instead of the old null-check. No change to the write paths themselves, to
`quick-blocker-drawer.tsx`, or to any other file.

**Verified myself, genuine red-then-green.** First dedicated test file for
this module (`vault-quick-fix-actions.spec.ts`, 4 tests, vitest convention -
this file imports the `@/` alias so the plain `node --experimental-strip-types`
`*.test.ts` convention can't resolve it, same documented limitation as every
other `@/`-importing action file in this codebase). Ran the new tests
against the pre-fix file first: 2 of 4 failed exactly as expected (asserting
the error message was NOT the old "Not signed in to this company." wording,
which the pre-fix code always returned regardless of cause) - confirmed they
actually exercise the bug, not a tautology. Applied the fix; re-ran - 4/4
passed. Full regression from `app/`: `npx vitest run` - **466/466 passed,
59/59 files** (up from 462/58: +1 new file, +4 new tests). The per-file
`*.test.ts` loop (no `--test` flag) - **27 files, 0 failures**, unchanged
(the new test file is a `.spec.ts`, not touched by this loop). `npm run
typecheck` - **0 errors**. `npx eslint .` - **0 errors**, same 3
pre-existing warnings. `npx next build` - **compiled successfully**, same
route table, `Proxy (Middleware)` present.

**Not independently verified:** against a real live Supabase transient-
failure scenario (no live Supabase credentials in this environment) - the
mocked-client test above exercises the exact code path, not a live network
blip. `update-actions.ts` (the other genuinely-untouched-since-2026-10-20
hyphenated file) was read in full and confirmed already correct (its one
`accept_tender_update_date` RPC call captures and logs `error` and redirects
with a real message) - not a new finding, recorded here so the next pass
doesn't re-spend time on it without reading this note first.

**Regression:** `app/app/tenders/[id]/vault-quick-fix-actions.ts` (~20 lines
changed/added: `requireCompanyId()`'s return type and body, both callers'
null-check replaced with an `ok` check); `app/app/tenders/[id]/vault-quick-
fix-actions.spec.ts` (new, 4 tests). No change to `quick-blocker-drawer.tsx`,
`lib/companyProfileUpdate.ts`, `lib/vaultDocuments.ts`, or any other file.

### Finding 147 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, low-moderate - `removePrivateTenderDocument()`'s own post-delete `count` read had no `error` captured, and a failed read of it forced the DESTRUCTIVE branch rather than the safe no-op one)

**Area:** Tender Workspace "Your private documents" card on a shared
tender (`app/app/tenders/[id]/general-actions.ts`'s
`removePrivateTenderDocument()`, called from `private-documents.tsx`'s
"Remove" button).

**How this was found.** Picked via the standing review's own "files with no
recent commits at all" heuristic, not a named backlog item: `private-
documents.tsx` sat at only 3 mentions in this doc and its own last commit
was 2026-10-23, so its one Server Action was read in full. Re-read the
2026-11-06 `091e884`/earlier pass's own write-up at line ~306 of
System-Status.md first (`general-actions.ts:269 ... not fixed - noted as a
real but minor candidate`) to avoid re-deriving an already-traced finding -
but that write-up is specifically about the `pack` read (the SECOND of the
two unchecked reads feeding this same `if` statement) failing, which really
is safe (`pack &&` makes a failed `pack` read skip the whole block, leaving
stale data - exactly as that entry describes). It never separately traced
what happens when the FIRST read - the `tender_private_documents` `count`
read right above it - fails instead, while `pack` succeeds. That's a
materially different, and worse, consequence.

**The bug.** After removing one private document, the function re-counts
how many the company has left on this tender, with `error` never
destructured at all:
```
const { count } = await supabase
  .from("tender_private_documents")
  .select("id", { count: "exact", head: true })
  .eq("company_id", companyId)
  .eq("tender_id", tenderId);
const { data: pack } = await supabase.from("tender_packs")...maybeSingle();
if (pack && (count ?? 0) === 0) {
  // wipe tender_packs.document_requirements/intake
} else if (pack) {
  // re-queue an extraction job, keeping the existing reading
}
```
On a transient failure of the `count` query, the Supabase client returns
`count: null` (and `data: null`), and `(count ?? 0) === 0` evaluates to
`true` - indistinguishable from "this really was the last private document,
genuinely down to zero now." If `pack`'s own read happens to succeed (the
common case: it's a separate, independent query, not the one that failed),
the code takes the "down to zero" branch and calls `supabase.from
("tender_packs").update({ document_requirements: null, intake: null })` -
wiping out this pack's already-extracted requirements/intake, discarding a
real, previously-computed reading, even though the company may still have
one or more other private documents on file that were never actually
recounted. The already-reviewed `pack`-read failure (same `if`, second half)
fails the OTHER way - `pack` falsy skips the whole block - so a prior pass
reading only that half concluded the failure mode here was "skipped once,
stale data," which is true for that read but is the exact opposite of what
actually happens when the `count` read is the one that fails.

**Consequence, traced to its real severity.** No RLS bypass, no cross-
tenant exposure, no money path - but real, user-visible data loss: a
transient Supabase blip immediately after a successful document removal can
silently discard a tender's already-extracted `document_requirements`/
`intake` (the parsed read of that tender's compliance-document needs) even
when the company's remaining private document(s) still fully support that
reading, forcing an unprompted, unexplained re-extraction the next time
anyone revisits the compliance/general-tender card - and, until something
re-triggers that re-extraction, a tender workspace that briefly shows "not
yet read" for a company's own tender despite nothing actually being wrong
with its documents.

**Fix:** captures `countError` from the count read, logs it
(`console.error`), and gates BOTH branches of the `if` on `!countError` -
not just the already-safe `pack &&` check. A failed count read now defers
the whole decision (same "stale, not falsely destructive" outcome already
accepted for the `pack`-read-failure case) instead of forcing the
destructive reset. A genuinely-zero count (no error) still takes the reset
branch exactly as before; a genuinely-nonzero count still takes the requeue
branch exactly as before - this only changes what happens when the read
itself errors.

**Verified myself, genuine red-then-green.** First dedicated test file for
this module (`general-actions.spec.ts`, 3 tests, vitest convention - this
file imports the `@/` alias and uses `next/navigation`'s `redirect()`, same
documented limitation as every other `@/`-importing action file). Ran the
new "count read fails" test against the pre-fix code first (temporarily
reverted just this block, kept the test file and the rest of the file as
they now stand): failed exactly as predicted - the destructive
`tender_packs.update({ document_requirements: ... })` call fired even
though the count read had errored (`expected 0 to have length but got 1`).
Restored the fix; re-ran - all 3 tests passed (the count-fails case takes
neither branch; a genuine 0 still resets; a genuine >0 still requeues).
Full regression from `app/`: `npx vitest run` - **469/469 passed, 60/60
files** (up from 466/59: +1 new file, +3 new tests). The per-file
`*.test.ts` loop (no `--test` flag) - **27 files, 0 failures**, unchanged
(the new test file is a `.spec.ts`). `npm run typecheck` - **0 errors**.
`npx eslint .` - **0 errors**, same 3 pre-existing warnings. `npx next
build` - **compiled successfully**, same route table, `Proxy (Middleware)`
present.

**Not independently verified:** against a real live Supabase transient-
failure scenario (no live Supabase credentials in this environment) - the
mocked-client test exercises the exact code path (a `count`-read error with
a successful `pack` read alongside it), not a live network blip. Also not
measured: how often this specific query pairing actually fails in
production (no live traffic data in this environment) - this is a
precautionary correctness fix for a real, reproducible logic error, not a
response to a confirmed-live incident.

**Regression:** `app/app/tenders/[id]/general-actions.ts`
(`removePrivateTenderDocument()`: ~10 lines changed - `count` read now
captures and logs `countError`, both `if`/`else if` branches gated on
`!countError`); `app/app/tenders/[id]/general-actions.spec.ts` (new, 3
tests). No change to `private-documents.tsx`, `saveGeneralAnswers()`, or any
other function in this file.

### Finding 148 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - `engine/worker/requirements.txt` pinned `pypdf==6.17.0`/`Pillow==12.3.0`, both with multiple known CVEs directly reachable through attacker-influenced uploads)

**Area:** `engine/worker/requirements.txt` (the bridge worker container's
pinned Python dependencies, `engine/worker/Dockerfile`) - specifically the
`pypdf` and `Pillow` pins, used throughout the pack/general/CV/OCR bridges
to parse real tender PDFs and uploaded vault scans/images.

**How this was found.** Picked as this pass's angle via the standing
directive's own "dependency/security audit" option: `npm audit --omit=dev`
on `app/` came back clean (0 vulnerabilities, matching the last time this
was checked, 2026-10-20), so the audit moved to the Python side, which this
doc's history shows has never had a dedicated dependency/CVE sweep. Ran
`pip-audit -r engine/worker/requirements.txt` against the exact pinned
versions (installed in this environment, confirmed identical to the pins:
`pypdf 6.17.0`, `Pillow 12.3.0`) - came back with 64 known vulnerabilities
across exactly those 2 packages (every other pinned/transitive dependency -
`python-docx`, `PyYAML`, `anthropic`, `pdfplumber`, `lxml`, `cryptography`,
`pydantic`, and 19 others - 0 vulnerabilities each, confirmed individually).

**The bugs, traced to why they matter here specifically, not just "CVEs
exist".** This is not a theoretical dependency-hygiene nit: both libraries
sit directly on attacker-influenced input paths in this codebase.
- **`pypdf==6.17.0`** - used by `pypdf.PdfReader`/`PdfWriter` in
  `engine/pack/pdf_merge.py`, `engine/general/fill_flat_pdf.py`,
  `engine/general/build_general_pack.py`, `engine/pack/assemble_pack.py`
  and `engine/print_financial.py` - every one of these reads a real tender
  PDF (a buyer's published document, or a company's own uploaded private
  document) that was never authored by this codebase. `6.17.0` carries
  multiple confirmed crafted-PDF denial-of-service advisories (long
  indirect-object-header parsing with no terminating whitespace
  (`PYSEC-2026-4153`); unbounded `/ToUnicode` CMap memory consumption during
  text extraction (`PYSEC-2026-4154`); oversized page-label memory blow-up
  (`PYSEC-2026-4160`); several more in the `6.18.0`-`6.21.4` range) - a
  malicious tender PDF (or malicious private document upload) could hang or
  exhaust memory on the worker that processes it.
- **`Pillow==12.3.0`** - used by `PIL.Image`/`ImageDraw`/`ImageSequence` in
  `engine/pack/assemble_pack.py`, `engine/general/build_general_pack.py`,
  `engine/ocr/scan_ocr.py` and `engine/pack/harness_pack.py` - the vault's
  own "scans uploaded as images are converted to PDF" path, i.e. a user-
  controlled image file. `12.3.0` carries multiple confirmed memory-safety
  advisories with no backported fix (every one fixed only in `13.0.0`):
  a buffer overread in the `P;2L`/`P;4L` raw decoders from a packed-row-size
  mismatch (`PYSEC-2026-4327`), a heap use-after-free when `libtiff` rejects
  a tag while encoding TIFF to an in-memory buffer (`PYSEC-2026-4328`), an
  out-of-bounds read in the rank-based filters on a zero-size image
  (`PYSEC-2026-4326`), and ~20 more (full list: `PYSEC-2026-4326` through
  `4343`, plus `CVE-2026-112390`-`112900`/`96638`/`96640`/`96778`). These are
  memory-corruption bug classes, not just DoS - worse in kind than the
  `pypdf` findings, on an equally real attacker-reachable path (any image a
  company uploads to the vault).

**Consequence, calibrated honestly.** No evidence of live exploitation in
this environment (no production logs, no incident) - this is the same
"precautionary hardening against a confirmed, reachable gap" tier this doc
has already used for other findings (e.g. Finding 37's `fill_a_forms.py`
control-character crash), not a response to an observed attack. The
severity rests on the advisories themselves being real, current (confirmed
against PyPI's actual published version history - `pypdf` through `7.0.0`,
`Pillow` through `13.0.0`, both consistent with today's date) and on the
input paths genuinely being attacker-influenced uploads, not synthetic
local files.

**Fix:** bumped `pypdf` to `6.21.4` (latest release still inside major
version 6 - deliberately did not jump to the newly-released `7.0.0`, to get
every known fix without taking on an unverified API-surface change at the
same time) and `Pillow` to `13.0.0` (every one of its advisories is fixed
only there, no 12.x backport exists, so there was no way to patch this one
without crossing the major version). Both are version-pin-only changes;
zero call sites touched.

**Verified myself, genuine before/after, not just a changelog read.**
1. Confirmed the "red" state directly: `pip-audit -r engine/worker/
requirements.txt` against the as-pinned versions - 64 known vulnerabilities,
2 packages, 0 in anything else.
2. Established a real baseline first: ran all 6 `engine/**/test_*.py` files
that actually import `pypdf`/`PIL` (`pack/test_pdf_merge.py`,
`cv/test_extract_cv_fields.py`, `discovery/test_kouga.py`,
`general/test_general_bridge.py`, `intake/test_manual_intake.py`,
`onboarding/test_classify_documents.py`) against the pre-fix, installed
`pypdf==6.17.0`/`Pillow==12.3.0` - all 6 passed (not assumed clean).
3. `pip install --upgrade pypdf==6.21.4 Pillow==13.0.0` in this same
environment (the sandbox had the exact pinned versions installed, so this
is a genuine upgrade, not a fresh install) - re-ran the same 6 files: all 6
still passed, including the pypdf-direct `test_pdf_merge.py`'s own stamped-
page/control-character checks and the Pillow-touching general/onboarding
bridge tests.
4. Ran the complete `engine/**/test_*.py` sweep repo-wide under the
upgraded packages - **84/84 files passed by real exit code** (not string-
grepped), matching this doc's documented baseline count exactly.
5. Re-ran the full 84-file sweep a second time with
`python3 -W error::DeprecationWarning` to surface any silently-changed
behaviour the exit-code check alone might miss - **zero files raised**,
across both packages' changed major/minor versions.
6. Confirmed the "green" state: `pip-audit -r engine/worker/requirements.txt`
against the now-edited file - **"No known vulnerabilities found"**.
No `app/` files were touched this pass (this is a pure `engine/worker/`
dependency-pin change) - `app/`'s own vitest/eslint/typecheck/build baseline
is therefore unaffected and was not re-run.

**What was and wasn't verified.** Not verified against a real Docker build
of `engine/worker/Dockerfile` (no Docker daemon in this environment) - the
upgrade was verified by installing the exact pinned versions directly into
this sandbox (which already carried the old pins) and running every real
test file that imports either library, not by rebuilding the actual worker
image. Not verified against a real malicious PDF/image reproducing any
specific advisory (these are upstream-confirmed, patched advisories with
public write-ups, not a locally-rediscovered bug - reproducing a heap UAF
or a crafted-PDF DoS by hand was judged unnecessary and out of proportion
for a version-pin fix with a clean upstream patch). Not measured: whether
either vulnerable code path has ever actually been hit by a real malicious
upload in production (no incident evidence either way) - this is
precautionary, not a response to a confirmed-live exploit.

**Regression:** `engine/worker/requirements.txt` only (`pypdf==6.17.0` →
`6.21.4`, `Pillow==12.3.0` → `13.0.0`, plus an explanatory comment). No
other file changed.

### Finding 149 (CONFIRMED, PARTIALLY FIXED, low - `npm audit`'s repeatedly-reconfirmed "0 vulnerabilities" on `app/`'s production dependencies had gone stale since the last time it was actually re-run, 2026-10-20; a fresh run today found 17 (7 production-reachable by `npm audit`'s own count), all transitive, all traced to zero real runtime attacker-reachable path)

**Area:** `app/package.json`/`package-lock.json` - specifically the
`shadcn` CLI tool (listed under `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`,
despite being a dev-time-only code generator) and `vitest` (a genuine
`devDependency`), via their own transitive dependency trees.

**How this was found.** This pass's angle was the standing directive's own
suggestion (b): re-check `app/package.json` the same way the immediately-
preceding pass (2026-11-07j) just did for `engine/worker/requirements.txt`
on the Python side. Every pass since 2026-10-20 has repeated "`npm audit
--omit=dev` on `app/` came back clean (0 vulnerabilities)" as an
unquestioned, reused fact (most recently 2026-11-07j, itself timestamped
today) - rather than trust that framing, re-ran it fresh. First confirmed
`node_modules` is genuinely in sync with the committed lockfile (`npm ci
--dry-run` - "up to date", nothing to install), so this is a real read of
what's actually pinned, not a stale local install: `npm audit --omit=dev`
returned **7 vulnerabilities (2 low, 4 moderate, 1 high)**, and the full
`npm audit` (including devDependencies) returned **17 (2 low, 12 moderate,
1 high, 2 critical)** - not the "0" every prior pass had been repeating.

**Traced to source, not just counted.** `npm ls body-parser`/`express`/
`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` showed exactly one path into all of the
production-side findings: `shadcn@4.22.1` (declared in `dependencies`) →
`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.32.1` → `express@5.3.0` → `body-parser@2.3.0`
(the HIGH: `GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828`, a trailing-bytes-after-compressed-body
DoS) plus `shadcn` → `deepmerge` (prototype-poisoning gadget,
`GHSA-gcqx-w48m-w2h4`, moderate) and `shadcn` → `ts-morph` → `minimatch`
(glob-amplification DoS, `GHSA-g3hv-75wg-m249`, moderate). The 2 critical
entries (`GHSA-5gmw-xhrv-c9v3`/`GHSA-85c8-ppgw-ccpr`, a prototype-pollution
gadget in `tinypool`'s worker options leading to RCE) are entirely inside
`vitest`'s own devDependency tree, never reachable via `--omit=dev`.

**Why this is NOT the same severity tier as Finding 148's pypdf/Pillow
case, checked rather than assumed.** Grepped the whole of `app/` (`.ts`/
`.tsx`, excluding `node_modules`) for any import of `shadcn`, `express`,
`body-parser`, `ts-morph`, `@typescript-eslint`, or `tinypool` - **zero
hits**. `shadcn` is a CLI invoked by hand (`npx shadcn add ...`, per
`AGENTS.md`'s own "Design system decisions" section) to generate
component source files during development; it, `ts-morph` and the
`@typescript-eslint`/`eslint-config-next` toolchain are never imported by
any file Next.js actually bundles, and `tinypool` is `vitest`'s own
internal test-worker pool, invoked only when a developer or CI runs the
test suite against a static, non-attacker-influenced config. Unlike
Finding 148's `pypdf`/`Pillow` (real libraries parsing real uploaded
files at runtime), none of these packages sit on any path a real visitor,
buyer, or uploaded document ever reaches - this is a real `npm audit`
finding with a traced, confirmed-absent production attack surface, not a
"nothing to see here" dismissal.

**Why the "0, unchanged since 2026-10-20" claim went stale - checked, not
just asserted.** `git log` confirms `package-lock.json` hasn't touched any
of these packages' versions since before 2026-10-24 (`14d1200`'s own diff
of that file contains no line for `shadcn`/`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`/
`body-parser`/`deepmerge`/`minimatch`/`tinypool`) - the exact same pinned
versions sat unchanged in the lockfile the whole time. Looked up each
advisory's real publish date via `api.osv.dev` (a live, independent
mirror of the GHSA database, not `npm audit`'s own cached feed) rather
than guessing: `GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828` (body-parser) published 2026-10-23 -
after the 2026-10-20 check, genuinely couldn't have been caught then;
`GHSA-g3hv-75wg-m249` (minimatch) published 2026-10-30 - after 2026-10-20
AND before 2026-11-07j's own "reconfirmed still 0" claim (today), meaning
that reconfirmation either wasn't actually re-run against a live feed or
missed it; `GHSA-gcqx-w48m-w2h4` (deepmerge) published 2026-09-18 - before
even the original 2026-10-20 check, which this entry cannot explain away
(either that original check was flawed, or npm's own advisory index
lagged the independent GHSA feed by over a month). Recording this
honestly rather than picking the explanation that looks best: this is a
live, in-the-wild demonstration of exactly the "npm audit's own database
can lag" risk the standing directive named by hypothesis, not a
reconstruction of it.

**Fix (partial, deliberately not forced).** `npm audit fix` (no `--force`)
resolved exactly 1 of the 7 production-reachable findings within the
semver ranges `package.json` already declares: it drops the vulnerable
`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`→`express`→`body-parser` chain entirely
(`shadcn`'s own dependency resolves through `@shadcn/registry 0.2.0 →
0.2.1` instead, which no longer pulls it), fixing the one HIGH. Confirmed
`shadcn` itself still runs afterward (`npx shadcn --version` → `4.23.0`,
still inside the declared `^4.22.1` range). The other 6 production-
reachable findings (`deepmerge`, `minimatch` via `ts-morph`) and the 10
devDependency-only findings (`minimatch` via `@typescript-eslint`/
`eslint-config-next`, `tinypool` via `vitest`) all require `npm audit fix
--force`, which `npm`'s own resolver says means: downgrading `shadcn` to
`1.0.0` (a major, almost-certainly-functionality-breaking downgrade of
the exact CLI tool `AGENTS.md` documents as pinned to the current "Nova"
preset), downgrading `eslint-config-next` to `15.5.29` (older than this
app's own `next@16.4.2`), or upgrading `vitest` to `5.1.0` (the exact
major version prompt 6's own `AGENTS.md` entry already explains was
avoided on purpose, because `vitest@5.x`'s peer dependency on `@types/
node@^22` conflicts with this project's pinned `@types/node@^20`). None
of these three were applied this pass - each is a real tooling-version
decision with a documented reason to stay put, not a drive-by call this
review loop should make unilaterally, and (per the reachability trace
above) none of the vulnerabilities they'd fix have any live production
exposure to begin with.

**Verified myself, genuine before/after.** 1) `npm ci --dry-run` first,
to confirm `node_modules` already matched the committed lockfile (no
stale local state). 2) `npm audit --omit=dev`/`npm audit` before the fix:
7/17 as above. 3) `npm audit fix` (no `--force`) - `package.json` itself
is byte-for-byte unchanged (`git diff package.json` - empty); only
`package-lock.json` changed (412 insertions, 744 deletions - entirely
transitive-tree changes, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`/`express`/
`body-parser`/`ajv`/`ejs`-adjacent packages removed, `@shadcn/registry`/
`typescript-eslint`-family packages bumped within range). 4) `npm audit
--omit=dev` after: **6 vulnerabilities (2 low, 4 moderate)** - the body-
parser HIGH gone, nothing else changed in kind. 5) Full regression:
`npm run typecheck` - 0 errors; `npx eslint .` - 0 errors, same 3 pre-
existing warnings; `npx vitest run` - **469/469 passed, 60/60 files**
(unchanged - this pass touched zero test files); the per-file `*.test.ts`
loop (no `--test` flag) - **27 files, 0 failures** (unchanged); `npx next
build` - **compiled successfully**, same 62-route table, `Proxy
(Middleware)` present.

**What was and wasn't verified.** Not independently verified that any of
the 3 remaining `--force`-only fixes would actually work without breaking
something - deliberately not attempted, for the tooling-pin reasons
above. Not verified whether `GHSA-gcqx-w48m-w2h4`'s 2026-09-18 publish
date genuinely predates when it became visible to `npm audit` specifically
(as opposed to the independent OSV mirror) - `osv.dev`'s `published` field
is the advisory's own origin-database publish date, not necessarily the
date `npm audit`'s specific feed picked it up; this entry reports the gap
honestly without claiming a single confirmed root cause for that one
advisory. Not verified against a live production deploy (no deploy
pipeline access in this environment) - this is a `package-lock.json`-only
change, and Vercel/the app's own build step installs from that lockfile,
so the fix should ship on the next deploy same as any other dependency
change, but that wasn't observed directly.

**Regression:** `app/package-lock.json` only (412 insertions, 744
deletions, entirely transitive dependency resolution - no direct
dependency version in `package.json` changed). No `app/` source file
touched.

### Finding 150 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - neither `npm audit` nor `pip-audit` was ever wired into this project's CI; every dependency-vulnerability finding in this doc (Findings 148, 149) was found by a human running the command by hand during a standing review pass, with no guarantee the next pass would ever re-run it)

**Area:** `.github/workflows/app-ci.yml` (Next.js app CI) and
`.github/workflows/bridge-worker-ci.yml` (engine/worker CI) - the two
workflows that gate every push to `main`.

**How this was found.** This pass's angle was the standing directive's own
suggestion (b): check whether the CI workflows actually run `pip-audit`/
`npm audit` as part of their gate, given that the 2026-11-07j and
2026-11-07k entries both found real, previously-unnoticed dependency
vulnerabilities (Findings 148 and 149) purely by a human running the
command by hand mid-pass. Read both `app-ci.yml` and `bridge-worker-ci.yml`
in full and grepped both (`grep -n "pip-audit\|npm audit"`) - **zero
hits in either file.** `app-ci.yml` runs `npm ci`/typecheck/lint/build/
vitest/the `*.test.ts` loop, and `bridge-worker-ci.yml`'s `smoke-test` job
installs `engine/worker/requirements.txt` and runs 60+ named test files -
neither workflow has ever once invoked a dependency-vulnerability scanner,
confirmed by reading both files start to finish, not by trusting either
workflow's own header comments (neither claims to run one, so this isn't
a case of a comment lying - it's a genuine, never-addressed gap).

**Why this matters, traced rather than assumed.** This is exactly the
failure mode Finding 149 itself lived through: the "`npm audit` --omit=dev
= 0 vulnerabilities" claim was repeated, unverified, across at least 4
consecutive standing-review-pass entries (2026-10-20 through 2026-11-07j)
before anyone actually re-ran the command and found it had gone stale by
7 production-reachable vulnerabilities, 2 of which (the HIGH `body-parser`
advisory, the `minimatch` moderate) were published in the gap between
checks. A CI gate that runs the scanner on every push closes that exact
gap - it doesn't depend on a human (or an AI review pass) remembering to
re-run a command that has no fixed cadence and, per this doc's own
history, can go unverified for weeks at a time.

**Fix.** Added `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` as a new step in
`app-ci.yml`, right after `npm ci`. `--audit-level=high` deliberately
means this does NOT fail on the 6 already-triaged, confirmed-production-
unreachable moderate/low findings Finding 149 left open on purpose
(`shadcn`'s own `deepmerge`/`minimatch` transitives - each one's real fix
is a tooling-version decision for Sarel, not something this review loop
or a CI gate should force) - it fails only on a genuinely new HIGH/
CRITICAL in a production dependency, which is the actual thing worth
blocking a push over. Added `pip-audit -r engine/worker/requirements.txt`
(installing `pip-audit` first) as a new step in `bridge-worker-ci.yml`'s
`smoke-test` job, right after the existing `pip install -r
engine/worker/requirements.txt` step, with no severity floor - the Python
pins are fully clean today (Finding 148 fixed them, 2026-11-07j), so there
is no equivalent "already-triaged, left open on purpose" exception to
carve out yet; a future CVE here should fail the job outright until
someone looks at it.

**Verified myself, genuine red-then-green.** For the npm step: ran `npm
audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` against the current, post-149-fix
`package-lock.json` first - **exit 0** (the 6 remaining findings are all
moderate/low, correctly under the `--audit-level=high` floor). Then
temporarily restored `package-lock.json` to its pre-Finding-149-fix state
(`git show f60bf0a:app/package-lock.json`, the commit immediately before
that fix) and re-ran the exact same command - **exit 1**, correctly
failing on the then-present `body-parser` HIGH (`GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828`).
Restored the current lockfile afterward (`git status --short
package-lock.json` confirmed byte-for-byte identical to HEAD, zero drift
introduced by the test). For the pip-audit step: ran `pip-audit -r
engine/worker/requirements.txt` directly against the current,
post-Finding-148-fix `requirements.txt` - **"No known vulnerabilities
found"**, exit 0 (not independently re-tested red against the pre-148
pins in this pass, since Finding 148's own entry already did that exact
red/green cycle for this file - re-deriving it again here would be
redundant, not a stronger verification). Both new workflow YAML files
parsed cleanly (`yaml.safe_load`). Full `app/` regression after the
change: `npm run typecheck` - 0 errors; `npx eslint .` - 0 errors, same 3
pre-existing warnings; `npx vitest run` - **469/469 passed, 60/60 files**
(unchanged); the per-file `*.test.ts` loop (no `--test` flag) - **27
files, 0 failures** (unchanged); `npx next build` - compiled
successfully, same route table, `Proxy (Middleware)` present. No
`engine/` Python file or test was touched, so the 84-file sweep wasn't
re-run; `pip-audit` itself was verified directly, which is the only thing
that changed on that side.

**What was and wasn't verified.** Not verified against a real GitHub
Actions run of either workflow (no Actions runner in this environment) -
verification is running the exact same commands these new steps invoke,
locally, against the exact files these workflows would check out, which
is the same standard this doc already uses for every other
`*-ci.yml`-adjacent fix. Not verified: whether a future `npm audit fix`
(or a manual `package.json` bump) could ever silently raise the
"accepted" moderate/low count past what `--audit-level=high` would still
let through as a NEW high/critical hiding inside a changed transitive
tree - this gate catches a new high/critical appearing on `main` as it
lands, not a slow drift inside a dependency a developer explicitly
chooses to bump; that's a smaller, longer-tail residual risk than the
"zero gate, zero cadence" one this fix closes. Not decided: whether
Sarel ever wants `--audit-level=high` tightened to `moderate` once the
`shadcn`/`eslint-config-next`/`vitest` version pins move - left as a
backlog note, not a call this pass makes unilaterally.

**Regression:** `.github/workflows/app-ci.yml` (+19 lines, one new step)
and `.github/workflows/bridge-worker-ci.yml` (+13 lines, one new step).
No `app/` or `engine/` source file touched.

### Finding 151 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, low/moderate - `/admin/notifications`'s own "Schedule & cron
health" tab, the one screen built specifically to tell Sarel whether the product's 10 critical
notification crons are actually running, would silently show every single workflow as "Never run
yet" instead of an error, if the one read that feeds it ever failed)

**Area:** `app/app/admin/notifications/page.tsx`, the `workflow_heartbeats` read that backs
`ScheduleHealthTable`.

**How this was found.** This pass's angle was (c) from the standing directive: pick a file in
`app/` or `engine/` never named anywhere in `System-Status.md`'s last ~15 entries, and read it
cold rather than chasing an already-exhausted named backlog item. Built the real exclusion set
first rather than guessing (every basename appearing anywhere in `System-Status.md`,
`QA-Edge-Case-Findings.md` or `app/AGENTS.md`, not just a skim) - every `engine/**/*.py` file
turned out already mentioned somewhere in this doc (the engine side of this review is now
genuinely exhaustively covered, not just mostly), but 36 `app/` files were genuinely untouched by
name, mostly vendored `components/ui/*` shadcn primitives with no logic to find a bug in. The one
real candidate with actual data-fetching logic: `app/admin/notifications/page.tsx`'s backing files
(`DispatchLogTab.tsx`, `TemplateGalleryTab.tsx`, `ScheduleHealthTable.tsx`, none individually
named before). The two client "Tab" components themselves are purely presentational (fed
already-computed, serializable rows) - the real logic, and the bug, is in the loader, `page.tsx`.

(Separately, this pass also re-checked the standing directive's own angle (b) - "re-read
`AI-Call-Quality-Standard.md` and spot-check an actual LLM call site... also suggested before,
not yet done" - against `git log`/this doc's own history before touching any LLM code, per the
standing instruction to verify a backlog item's "not yet done" framing rather than trust it: the
2026-11-01 entries (line ~7515, line ~7574) already closed this out across all 5 real LLM call
sites in the codebase (`scope_llm.py`, `generate_narrative.py`, `extract_cv_fields.py`,
`classify_documents.py`, `company_documents.py`), each one read against the standard by name, one
real fix found (`scope_llm.py`'s `verify_evidence_quotes()`) and the other 4 confirmed clean or
already-flagged-as-acknowledged-follow-up (the single-pass gap `AI-Call-Quality-Standard.md`'s own
opening paragraph already names as separate, pre-existing scope). Re-deriving that sweep a third
time would not have been a stronger result than this doc's own existing entries - recorded here
so a future pass doesn't repeat the same stale "not yet done" framing a fourth time.)

**The bug, traced to its real consequence.** `page.tsx` fetches two independent Supabase reads in
one `Promise.all` - `notification_logs` (whose `error` is correctly captured, logged, and surfaced
as a banner) and `workflow_heartbeats` (whose `error` was destructured off entirely:
`const [{ data: logData, error: logError }, { data: heartbeatData }] = await Promise.all([...])`
- `heartbeatData`'s own `error` was never even bound to a name, let alone checked). A failed
`workflow_heartbeats` read left `heartbeatData` `undefined`, so `heartbeatByKey` built from it is
an empty `Map`, so every one of the 10 entries in `WORKFLOW_REGISTRY` resolves
`heartbeatStatusFor(entry, null, nowMs)` - confirmed directly against `lib/workflowRegistry.ts`'s
own code and its own already-passing unit test (`workflowRegistry.spec.ts`, "never_run when no
heartbeat row exists yet") - which returns `"never_run"` unconditionally whenever `row` is `null`.
This is the exact "unprotected/discarded Supabase call whose error is silently treated as a
false-safe 'nothing here' state" shape this whole review track has been naming as its dominant bug
class, on the one screen whose entire stated purpose (per its own on-page copy) is telling an
admin "whether it actually ran" for the 10 cron workflows that are this product's whole
deadline/compliance/discovery notification safety net. A transient read failure (RLS hiccup,
connection blip) would read, indistinguishably from the genuine case, as "every single one of our
10 critical crons has never run even once" - the single most alarming possible false reading this
specific page could show, with nothing on the page (unlike the sibling `notification_logs` read
two lines above it) to say the read itself had failed.

**Severity, reasoned rather than inflated.** This is an internal `/admin/*` page, already gated by
`app/app/admin/layout.tsx`'s own `is_platform_admin()` RPC check (confirmed by reading that file -
no signed-in company account without admin rights can reach this page at all, so there is no
security/RLS exposure here, only a correctness/visibility one for an actual platform admin). No
data is lost or corrupted - the underlying `workflow_heartbeats` rows are untouched; this is purely
a misleading read on one monitoring screen. Not escalated to "critical" because nothing downstream
of this page's own render ever consults `heartbeatByKey` - no automated alert or gate depends on
it, only a human looking at the tab.

**Fix:** captured and logged `heartbeatError` the same way `logError` already was, and added a
second, clearly-worded banner (parallel to the existing `logError` banner, not replacing it) that
tells the admin specifically that the heartbeat read failed and that the Schedule & cron health tab
below it may therefore wrongly show every workflow as "Never run yet." Deliberately did not change
`heartbeatStatusFor()` itself or try to distinguish "never run" from "read failed" inside the table
component - that would mean inventing a new status value and touching the already-tested,
already-correct pure function and its own test file, for a presentation-only distinction the new
banner already covers at the page level. `scheduleRows` still computes exactly as before when the
read succeeds; only the failure path changed.

**Verified myself.** No red/green test possible for this specific file: it is a Server Component
page with `next/headers`/Supabase-server imports at module scope (same already-documented
limitation as every other RSC-page finding in this doc, e.g. Finding 144's `document-scan/page.tsx`
- no existing test file, and this repo's own `node:test` convention cannot resolve the `@/` alias
this file needs). The downstream consequence the fix depends on *is* independently, already
verified: `workflowRegistry.spec.ts`'s existing "never_run when no heartbeat row exists yet" test
(re-ran directly, passes) confirms `heartbeatStatusFor(entry, null, nowMs)` really does return
`"never_run"` for a null row, which is exactly the state the discarded error produced - so the bug
this entry describes is not asserted from reading alone, it's the directly-tested behavior of the
one function the discarded error flows into. Full regression: `npm run typecheck` - 0 errors;
`npx eslint .` - 0 errors, same 3 pre-existing warnings; `npx vitest run` - **469/469 passed, 60/60
files** (unchanged - no test file touched); the per-file `*.test.ts` loop (no `--test` flag) -
**27 files, 0 failures** (unchanged); `rm -rf .next && npm run build` - compiled successfully, same
route table, `Proxy (Middleware)` present.

**What was and wasn't verified.** Not independently verified against a real live Supabase
transient-failure scenario for this specific query (no live Supabase credentials in this
environment) - the fix's correctness rests on reading the exact code path directly (the discarded
`error` destructure, confirmed in the pre-fix diff) plus the already-passing, already-existing unit
test for the one function that consumes the discarded state, not a live reproduction of a
Postgres/RLS blip. Not measured: how often this specific read has actually failed in production (no
incident evidence either way) - this is a precautionary correctness/visibility fix for a real,
traced logic gap, not a response to a confirmed-live incident, same honesty standard this doc uses
for comparable findings.

**Regression:** `app/app/admin/notifications/page.tsx` only (+8/-1 lines - one destructured
`error` field, one `console.error` line, one new banner block). No other file touched.

### Finding 152 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, significant - the "Bid Pack Compilation Complete" email has
never actually sent in production, for any company, since it shipped - the worker container had
no `node` binary at all, and `.dockerignore` separately excluded the `app/` directory the render
script lives in)

**Area:** `engine/worker/Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, consumed by `engine/notify/send_pack_ready_email.py`'s `_render()`.

**How this was found.** This pass's angle was (b) from the standing directive: read
`engine/worker/Dockerfile` end to end and cross-check every package/tool it installs against what
the Python code in `engine/` actually imports or shells out to - "is anything installed-but-unused,
or (worse) used-but-not-installed." Grepped every `subprocess.run`/`subprocess.Popen` call across
`engine/` (non-test files) against the Dockerfile's apt packages: `pdftotext`/`pdftoppm`/
`pdfimages`/`pdfinfo` (all `poppler-utils`, already installed), `soffice` (LibreOffice, already
installed), `tesseract` (already installed) all matched cleanly. One call didn't: `send_pack_ready_email.py`'s
`_render()` shells out to `["node", "--experimental-strip-types", RENDER_SCRIPT, ...]` - and `node`
appears nowhere in the Dockerfile at all (confirmed by grep, not a skim).

**The bug, traced to its real consequence, not assumed from the missing apt package alone.**
Two independent, each-on-its-own-fatal gaps:

1. **`.dockerignore` excluded the entire `app/` directory** from the Docker build context (a single
   `app` line, with the comment "keep the Next.js app... out of the image"), predating this
   notification feature (built 2026-10-27, the "notification engine migration" entry) by weeks. The
   render script (`app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.ts`) and its own `cwd`
   (`APP_DIR = <repo>/app`, which `_render()`'s `subprocess.run(..., cwd=APP_DIR, ...)` passes) never
   existed in the built image at all.
2. **The Dockerfile never installed a `node` binary**, in the first place - its apt packages are
   LibreOffice/poppler-utils/Tesseract/fonts only. Even if (1) were fixed on its own, Debian
   bookworm's own `nodejs` apt package is 18.x, which doesn't have `--experimental-strip-types` at
   all (added in Node 22.6) - a plain `apt-get install nodejs` would still fail, just with a
   different error.

Reproduced directly rather than inferred from reading alone: mirrored the exact file set
`engine/worker/Dockerfile`'s own pre-fix `COPY` lines put into the image (`engine/`, `fingerprints/`,
`templates/`, `config/test_companies/`, `config/discipline_taxonomy.json` - nothing from `app/`) into
a scratch directory, then ran the real `send_pack_ready_email()` against it with a fake Supabase
client. It raised `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '<mirrored>/srv/app'`
(Python's `subprocess.run` checks `cwd` exists before even trying to exec `node`) - caught by the
function's own top-level `except Exception`, recorded as a `system_alerts.record(..., "warning",
...)` row, and swallowed. Confirmed the same call against the FULL dev-sandbox repo checkout (which
happens to have both `node` on `PATH` and a real `app/` directory) renders successfully - which is
exactly why this has never been caught by any prior verification run in this environment: every
test of this code path so far has necessarily run from a full checkout, never from the actual
stripped-down image the Dockerfile builds, so the gap was invisible to every environment this
feature was ever "verified" in.

**Practical consequence.** The pack job itself always succeeds (the pack is real, assembled, and
already uploaded by the time `send_pack_ready_email()` runs) - only the notification fails, exactly
as the function's own docstring says it's designed to tolerate. But because the render failure
happens *before* `claim_notification()` is ever called (deliberately, per this file's own
2026-10-30 fix, so a render failure doesn't burn the one-time claim token) and this job id never
runs again once the pack reaches "ready," the practical effect is not a delay - it's a **permanent,
100%-reproducible loss of this exact email for every pack, for every company**, since the feature
shipped, assuming `RESEND_API_KEY` is configured in the worker's real environment (a prior pass,
2026-11-05, confirmed the key is live and valid). This is also the direct, structural answer to a
backlog item several prior `System-Status.md` entries (2026-11-05 through -07i) carried forward
unresolved as "whether `send_pack_ready_email.py`'s own fix fires clean in its real always-on-worker
environment... no visibility into that host's logs from here" - resolved here by reading the
Dockerfile and `.dockerignore` structurally, which was always possible and didn't need host log
access at all.

**Severity, reasoned not inflated.** Not a security/RLS issue (no cross-tenant exposure), not data
loss (the pack itself is correct and already delivered via the normal in-app download), not a
money-path issue. But it is a complete, silent failure of a real, shipped, customer-facing
notification feature in production since 2026-10-27 - every "your bid pack is ready" email a real
company should have received has instead become a `system_alerts` warning row nobody is known to
have been checking (the same `/admin/notifications` dispatch log this doc's Finding 151 already
covers would show these as failed sends, if anyone looked; `notification_logs` itself never gets a
row at all for this path, since the claim/send/log sequence never reaches that point). Called
"significant," not "critical," because the underlying work product (the pack) is unaffected and
every recipient can still see "Pack Ready" status live in the Tender Workspace itself - this is a
missed proactive notification, not a missed or corrupted deliverable.

**Fix.** `.dockerignore`: replaced the single blanket `app` exclusion with three precise ones
(`app/node_modules`, `app/.next`, `app/.env*` with `!app/.env*.example`) - Docker's own documented
rule is that a file can't be re-included once a parent directory is excluded, so the fix had to stop
excluding `app` wholesale rather than try to carve out an exception under it. `engine/worker/Dockerfile`:
added Node.js 22 via the NodeSource apt repo (matching `app-ci.yml`'s own Node 22 pin, and clearing
the `--experimental-strip-types` version floor Debian's own `nodejs` package doesn't meet), and two
new `COPY app/lib app/lib` / `COPY app/scripts app/scripts` lines - not the whole `app/` directory,
since `app/node_modules` (796 MB) and `app/.next` (157 MB) are both still excluded and nothing under
`app/` the render script's own import chain actually reaches at runtime needs an npm package: its
one npm-importing dependency (`notificationEngine.ts`'s `@supabase/supabase-js`, pulled in by
`emailTemplatesTier1.ts`'s `import type { NotificationEmail } from "./notificationEngine.ts"`) is a
type-only import, which this codebase has already independently confirmed elsewhere (`pack-review-logic.ts`'s
own comment, this doc's prompt-8-step-3 entry) is fully erased by `--experimental-strip-types` with
zero runtime module resolution attempted - confirmed again here empirically, not just cited.

**Verified myself, genuine red-then-green.** Red: the mirrored pre-fix image layout (above) - real
`FileNotFoundError` every time, caught and swallowed into a `system_alerts.record(...)` call
(captured via a stub in the repro harness rather than a real DB write). Green: added only
`app/lib` and `app/scripts` (no `node_modules`, no `package.json`) to the same mirrored layout and
re-ran `node --experimental-strip-types app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.ts '<json>'` directly -
exit 0, correct `{"subject", "html", "text"}` JSON on stdout. Re-ran the full `send_pack_ready_email()`
repro against that same post-fix mirrored layout with a fake Supabase client (recipients, tender,
company, `claim_notification`, `record_notification_sent` all stubbed) - **zero `system_alerts.record()`
calls**, confirming the render step that used to fail every time now succeeds end to end. Ran the
existing `engine/notify/test_send_pack_ready_email.py` (mocks `_render()`/`_send_via_resend()` at
the Python level, so unaffected by this Dockerfile/`.dockerignore`-only change) - **0 failures**,
confirming no regression at the unit level, which this change was never expected to touch (no
Python source file was edited). Also pushed the fix branch (`fix/worker-pack-ready-email-node`) to
GitHub and manually dispatched the real `bridge-worker-ci.yml` workflow against it
(`workflow_dispatch`, since this workflow only auto-triggers on `push` to `main`) specifically to
get its `container-build` job to run a REAL `docker build -f engine/worker/Dockerfile .` on a real
GitHub Actions runner (something this sandbox cannot do - no Docker daemon here) - see this pass's
own `System-Status.md` entry for that run's actual result, recorded there rather than guessed at
here since it may complete after this file is written.

**What was and wasn't verified.** Not verified: a real live Resend send from inside the fixed image
(this repro's `_send_via_resend()` call used a fake API key and either way talks to Resend's real
endpoint, so this was deliberately exercised only as far as confirming the render step itself, not
re-verified as a live send - that was already independently confirmed working, with a real key,
by the 2026-10-27/2026-11-05 entries, and this fix touches nothing on that side). Not verified:
whether the NodeSource install step itself (`curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | bash -`)
succeeds inside Railway's own build environment specifically, as opposed to a GitHub Actions
runner or this sandbox - both of the latter have unrestricted outbound HTTPS by default, and
Railway's own documented build environment doc doesn't suggest otherwise, but this is the one part
of the fix resting on the same network reachability Railway's build already needs for `apt-get
update`/`pip install` to work at all, not a newly introduced assumption. Not independently measured:
how many real packs have gone "ready" since 2026-10-27 and therefore how many real pack-ready
emails this bug has actually cost - no application-level metric for this exists, and this pass's own
budget went to the structural fix and its verification, not a historical `pack_generation_jobs`
count (left as a natural follow-up for whoever reviews the PR, not guessed at here).

**Regression:** `.dockerignore` (+15/-4 lines) and `engine/worker/Dockerfile` (+22 lines, 2 new
`COPY` lines, one apt install extended) only. No Python source file touched, no `app/` source file
touched.

**Not pushed directly to `main`** - opened as a PR instead (`fix/worker-pack-ready-email-node`),
per the standing guardrail's "anything larger" framing: this changes what packages/runtime the
production worker image installs and what source tree it copies in, and the one thing that would
fully confirm it (an actual `docker build` of the real image) cannot be run in this sandbox at all
(no Docker daemon here, the same standing gap every prior Dockerfile-adjacent entry in this doc has
named) - the real build-and-boot confirmation this pass could get came from manually dispatching
the repo's own `bridge-worker-ci.yml` `container-build` job on GitHub Actions against the fix
branch, not from a direct push with an unverified Docker-build risk.

### Finding 153 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, minor-but-real - `render-pack-ready-email.ts` had zero test
coverage of the one way it is actually run, so the exact bug class Finding 152 just fixed could
recur with every check green)

**Area:** `app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.ts`, consumed by
`engine/notify/send_pack_ready_email.py`'s `_render()`. Adjacent to, but distinct from, Finding 152
(the Dockerfile/`.dockerignore` fix in PR #181).

**How this was found.** This pass's angle was (c) from the standing directive: read every
`.github/workflows/*.yml` file end to end and look for a trigger (path filter, cron, condition)
that has drifted from what the code it's supposed to protect actually looks like now. All 15
workflow files read in full. The 13 schedule-only notification workflows
(`compliance-alerts`/`corrigendum-alerts`/`daily-digest`/`daily-discovery`/`deadline-reminders`/
`founder-digest`/`onboarding-nudges`/`operational-alerts`/`returnables-digest`/`scout-alerts`/the
two reachability test workflows/`test-resend-setup`) are all cron-only with no path filter to drift
- checked their stagger (deliberately offset minutes, documented in each file's own comments) and
found no overlap or gap. The two path-filtered workflows (`app-ci.yml`, `bridge-worker-ci.yml`) are
where a path filter actually could drift from the code.

**The gap.** `bridge-worker-ci.yml`'s own `on.push.paths` list (`engine/**`, `templates/forms/**`,
`templates/general_samples/**`, `fingerprints/**`, `config/discipline_taxonomy.json`,
`app/supabase/migrations/**`, `.dockerignore`, plus itself) does **not** include `app/lib/**` or
`app/scripts/**` - but `engine/worker/Dockerfile`, on the still-open PR #181
(`fix/worker-pack-ready-email-node`, confirmed by reading that branch's own diff:
`gh api repos/sareljvr2024/tender-tool/pulls/181/files` shows only `.dockerignore` and
`engine/worker/Dockerfile` touched), adds exactly those two directories as new `COPY` lines because
the worker image's render step now genuinely depends on them. Once #181 merges, a future change to
`app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.ts` or anything in its import chain (most directly
`app/lib/emailTemplatesTier1.ts`) will **not** trigger `bridge-worker-ci.yml` at all - no
`container-build` run, no real `docker build`, no re-verification that the render step still works
inside the actual stripped-down worker image. `app-ci.yml` does already trigger on both paths
(its own filter is the much broader `app/**`), but confirmed its steps (`typecheck`, `lint`,
`build`, the `*.spec.ts`/`*.test.ts` loops) never actually invoke
`node --experimental-strip-types app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.ts` the way the real worker
does - grepped the whole repo for `render-pack-ready-email` (`Grep`, excluding
`app/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo`) and found exactly 5 hits: this doc, `System-Status.md`, the Python
caller, the script itself, and `emailTemplatesTier1.ts` - no test file anywhere exercised it as a
subprocess before this pass. That matters because TypeScript's own typecheck, and Next.js's own
build, both resolve a plain value import of a type-only symbol just fine (full type information is
available to both) - `--experimental-strip-types` cannot: it has no type information and can only
erase declarations the TypeScript *syntax* itself marks type-only (`import type { X }`, or an
inline `type` keyword). So a future edit that silently changes
`emailTemplatesTier1.ts`'s own `import type { NotificationEmail } from "./notificationEngine.ts"`
to a plain value import would typecheck clean, build clean, pass every existing unit test - and
then fail exactly the way Finding 152 did, silently, in production only, the first time the worker
actually tries to render a real pack-ready email.

**Reproduced the exact failure mode, not assumed.** Temporarily changed that one import in
`app/lib/emailTemplatesTier1.ts` from `import type { NotificationEmail }` to
`import { NotificationEmail }` and ran the new test directly
(`node --experimental-strip-types app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.test.ts`): real
`SyntaxError: The requested module './notificationEngine.ts' does not provide an export named
'NotificationEmail'`, all 3 subtests fail, exit code 1. Reverted the import
(confirmed `git diff app/lib/emailTemplatesTier1.ts` empty afterward) and re-ran: all 3 subtests
pass, exit code 0. Genuine red-then-green on the exact bug shape this finding is about.

**Fix.** Added `app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.test.ts` - a `node:test` file that spawns the
real script as a real child process (`node --experimental-strip-types
app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.ts '<json>'`, `cwd` set to `app/`, matching
`send_pack_ready_email.py`'s own `_render()` call exactly), not an `import` of it (the script's own
unconditional `main()` reads `process.argv[2]` and calls `process.exit()`, so importing it directly
under a test runner would kill the test process on the wrong argv). Covers: a real render with a
realistic `packReadyEmail()` payload (asserts exit 0 and the `{subject, html, text}` shape, with the
reference/buyer/page-count actually present in the output); no `argv[2]` at all (exit 1, `Usage` on
stderr, nothing on stdout); unparsable JSON (exit 1, parse-error message on stderr, nothing on
stdout) - the script's own documented error contract, now actually checked rather than only
described in a comment. Picked up automatically by `app-ci.yml`'s existing per-file `*.test.ts`
loop, which already triggers on any `app/**` push today, independent of whether PR #181 has merged.

**Verified for real, not just asserted.** Ran the new test file directly both before (green) and
during the deliberate-break red state above. Then ran the full baseline: `npm run typecheck`
(clean), `npx eslint .` (0 errors, the same 3 pre-existing warnings as the standing baseline -
`Logo.tsx` x2, `analytics/page.tsx` x1), `npx vitest run` (**60 files, 469 tests, all passing** -
unchanged from the standing baseline, since this change added no `.spec.ts` file), and the full
per-file `*.test.ts` node loop with no `--test` flag (**28 files now** - the standing baseline's 27
plus this new one - **0 failures**, checked by real exit code, not a string grep).

**What this does NOT close.** This test only catches the "non-erasable import" bug shape (the one
TypeScript alone can't catch). It does **not** replace a real `docker build` as the only thing that
can confirm the Dockerfile's own `COPY`/`apt-get` lines are still correct once PR #181's actual
change lands - that gap (`bridge-worker-ci.yml`'s path filter missing `app/lib/**`/`app/scripts/**`)
is **not fixed by this pass**, deliberately: `engine/worker/Dockerfile` on `main` right now does
**not** copy `app/lib` or `app/scripts` at all (that only happens on PR #181's own unmerged branch),
so adding those paths to `bridge-worker-ci.yml` on `main` today would trigger a real `docker build`
job on every unrelated `app/lib`/`app/scripts` push for a dependency the current image doesn't
actually have yet - a path filter that doesn't match what the code it protects currently looks
like, which is exactly the kind of drift this angle was looking for in the other direction. The
right fix is for whoever merges PR #181 to add `app/lib/**` and `app/scripts/**` to
`bridge-worker-ci.yml`'s own `on.push.paths` in the same change (or immediately after) - named here
explicitly so it isn't missed, not implemented speculatively against code that isn't on `main` yet.
This is a genuine, if narrower, risk than it looks: this new unit test (and `app-ci.yml`'s existing
`typecheck`/`build`) would catch an import-shape regression, but neither would catch a regression in
the Dockerfile's own `COPY` lines or apt/NodeSource install step itself (e.g. a future `app/lib`
file added to the real import chain that isn't under the two `COPY` lines PR #181 adds) - only a
real `docker build`, gated on the right paths, catches that.

**Regression:** one new file, `app/scripts/render-pack-ready-email.test.ts` (+93 lines). No existing
file changed (the deliberate-break-and-revert during verification left `emailTemplatesTier1.ts`
byte-for-byte unchanged - confirmed via `git diff`, empty).

**Pushed directly to `main`** - small, narrow, additive (one new test file), does not touch
RLS/money paths/hard-stop gates, and does not change what the production worker image
installs/copies (that remains scoped to PR #181, untouched by this pass).

### Finding 154 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - DBSA's own procurement page currently lists one real
RFP twice under the same reference number, which gave both rows the identical `ocid` and would let
this engine's per-release scoring/seeding silently score and report the same tender twice in one
run, with whichever copy is written last overwriting the other's `discovered_opportunities` row)

**Area:** `engine/discovery/dbsa_procurement.py` (`normalize()`/`fetch_releases()`), reached from
`gov_sources.py`'s `ALL_SOURCES` -> `watch_new_tenders.py`'s fan-out/scoring -> `seed_supabase_opportunities.py`.

**How this was found.** This pass's angle was a subsystem-level read of the Discovery fan-out/
scoring path as one coherent system (`run_discovery.py`, `watch_new_tenders.py`, `assess_tender.py`,
`company_profiles.py`, `discovery_downgrades.py`, `seed_supabase_opportunities.py`,
`download_discovered_documents.py`, `score_outlook.py`, `taxonomy.py`) - all read start to finish,
cross-checked against each other's own contracts, plus the full existing test suite for that path
re-run for real (all green: `test_discovery_fanout.py`, `test_discovery_downgrades.py`,
`test_taxonomy.py`, `test_score_outlook*.py`, `test_assess_tender.py`,
`test_download_discovered_documents.py`, `test_gov_sources.py`). That slice itself came up clean.

The real finding came from following up on `kouga.py`'s own very recent fix (2026-11-06,
`cb35c24`: "Kouga reuses the same Ref No for an original listing and its later re-advertisement" ->
both got the identical `ocid`, fixed with `_disambiguate_reused_refs()`). Checked whether the same
*shape* of bug (a direct-buyer reader building its `ocid` from the raw, human-entered reference
number alone, with no secondary unique identifier) exists in any of this pipeline's other direct
readers - not assumed, checked each one's own `ocid=` line:
`transnet_etenders.py` (`rowKey`, a site-internal id - safe), `eskom_bulletin.py` (`TENDER_ID`, a
site-internal id - safe), `capetown_procurement.py` (`detail_id or ref` - prefers a site-internal
id, only falls back to `ref` when the row has no detail link - low risk), `cidb_tenders.py`
(`tender_ID`, a site-internal id - safe, and confirmed live: 25 distinct, non-null ids today, zero
collisions). Five readers build `ocid` from the raw reference alone, the same pre-fix shape as
Kouga: `dbsa_procurement.py`, `sars_procurement.py`, `lephalale.py`, `vaal_central_water.py`,
`randwater.py`.

**Checked live, not assumed, for each of the five - confirmed on real, current data, not a
hypothetical.** Ran each reader's own `fetch_releases()` against the real live site through this
sandbox's outbound proxy and counted distinct `ocid`s vs. total rows:
- `dbsa_procurement.py`: **10 open rows, only 9 distinct ocids** - a genuine collision, confirmed
  real: ref `RFP185/2026` appears as two separate table rows right now - "RFP 185/2026: ... Tender
  Volume , Addendum 01 Onsite Compulsory Briefing Session ..." (published 2 Nov) and "RFP185/2026:
  ... Tender Volume Onsite Compulsory Tender Briefing ..." (published 28 Oct) - same closing date
  (23 Nov 23:55), a genuine addendum re-listing of the same RFP, not a parsing artefact.
  **This is the one fixed this pass** (below).
- `sars_procurement.py`: 2 open rows today, both distinct - no live collision found (too small a
  sample to rule the risk out, the code shape is still identical to Kouga's pre-fix one).
- `lephalale.py` / `vaal_central_water.py`: unreachable from this sandbox right now (`lephalale.gov.za`
  reset the connection after 3 retries; `vaal_central_water`'s own site returned a flat 403) - the
  same sandbox-vs-real-network gap this project has already named for `randwater.py`
  (`gov_sources.py`'s own comment: confirmed only reachable from a GitHub Actions runner, not this
  sandbox). Not checked live this pass for that reason, not because the risk doesn't apply.
- `randwater.py`: same reachability gap, not checked live.

**The real consequence, traced through the pipeline, not assumed from the collision alone.**
`gov_sources.merge()`'s own "never fold two rows of the same source into each other" rule (so
SANRAL's bid and its own lot aren't merged) means merge() does **not** collapse the two DBSA rows
either - both pass straight through to the merged release list, still sharing one `ocid`. From
there: `watch_new_tenders.py`'s `release_key()` (`ocid` first) treats them as the SAME release, so
`fan_out()`'s Pass 1 loop creates one shared `seen` entry and schedules BOTH rows into `prepared`
pointing at that same shared entry object; Pass 3 then scores every company against the FIRST
row's reading, then re-scores (and overwrites `entry["companies"][key]`) against the SECOND row's
reading - double the document fetch/scoring cost for every affected tender, and TWO separate
`out` entries (same ocid, slightly different title/description text) both flow into
`seed_supabase_opportunities.seed()`, whose `(company_id, ocid)` upsert means the SECOND one
processed silently overwrites the FIRST's `discovered_opportunities` row and reasons within the
same run - and, worse, because `seed()` re-reads `_existing()` fresh for each `company_results`
entry in the same call, the second row's `discovery_downgrades.flag_update()` check runs against
the row the FIRST one *just wrote* a moment earlier in the same run, which could raise a spurious
same-run "downgrade" flag purely from this duplicate-listing artifact if the two near-identical
texts ever happened to classify differently - exactly the kind of false signal
`discovery_downgrades.py` exists to prevent, not cause.

**Fix**, mirroring `kouga.py`'s own `_disambiguate_reused_refs()` (2026-11-06) in shape: added
`dbsa_procurement._disambiguate_reused_refs()`, called at the end of `fetch_releases()` (after the
`is_closed` filter, same spot Kouga's fix runs). Only a colliding `ocid` is touched - every row
whose base ocid is unique keeps exactly the ocid it always had, so this cannot re-trigger a "new
tender" alert for any of DBSA's other, never-ambiguous tenders. DBSA's own page has no stable
per-row detail URL to suffix with the way Kouga's own per-card link let that fix do it (every DBSA
row shares the one list page as its `source_url`) - `published_date` is the field that actually
differed between the two real duplicate rows, so it is used as the suffix instead; a short hash of
the title is the last-resort fallback for the (unseen in practice) case where even `published_date`
collides too, so two such rows are never silently re-merged into one.

**Verified genuinely, red-then-green, against the real live collision.** Added
`test_dbsa_reused_ref_gets_distinct_ocids_not_a_collision()` to `test_gov_sources.py`, with a fixture
(`DBSA_REUSED_REF_HTML`) trimmed directly from the real live duplicate rows above, run through
`dbsa_procurement.fetch_releases()` itself (not just the disambiguation function in isolation) via
a monkeypatched `fetch_list()`. Ran it before the fix: **red** - both rows shared one ocid, the
two new "do NOT share an ocid" assertions failed. Applied the fix, re-ran: **green** - all 4 new
checks pass, plus the pre-existing `DBSA_TABLE_HTML` fixture (two genuinely different refs) run
through the same `fetch_releases()` entry point still gets plain, unsuffixed ocids. Then re-ran
`dbsa_procurement.fetch_releases()` against the REAL live site again, post-fix: **10 open rows, 10
distinct ocids now** (`dbsa-procurement:RFP185/2026:2026-11-02T00:00:00+02:00` and
`...:2026-10-28T00:00:00+02:00`) - the live collision is genuinely closed, not just the synthetic
fixture. Full regression: the complete `test_gov_sources.py` suite - **ALL PASSED**; the full
`engine/` per-file test loop (`for f in find . -maxdepth 2 -name "test_*.py"`, real exit codes) -
**84 files, 0 failures**, matching the standing baseline exactly (no other file touched).

**What this does NOT close.** The same architectural risk (an `ocid` built from the raw reference
alone, no secondary disambiguator) remains unverified-but-unfixed in `sars_procurement.py`,
`lephalale.py`, `vaal_central_water.py` and `randwater.py` - named here as a concrete, scoped
backlog item for a future pass (ideally one that can reach `lephalale.gov.za`/
`vaal_central_water`'s site, or dispatches a check from a GitHub Actions runner the way this
project's own Dockerfile-shaped verifications already do for `randwater.py`), not fixed
speculatively against code with no demonstrated live collision - the standing directive's own
"don't force it" rule.

**Regression:** `engine/discovery/dbsa_procurement.py` (+46 lines, one new function + its call site),
`engine/discovery/test_gov_sources.py` (+53 lines, one new fixture + one new test function). No
other file touched.

**Pushed directly to `main`** - small, narrow (one reader's own de-duplication logic), does not
touch RLS/money paths/hard-stop gates, and does not change what the production worker image
installs/copies.

### Finding 155 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - `confirm_pack.py`'s own inline `initial_graduated` parsing never got the non-string-date guard `years_experience_at()` was fixed for (Finding 138), so an uncaught `TypeError` from the real pack-confirmation gate was wrongly escalated from a routine, user-actionable refusal into what `process_pack_jobs.py`'s own caller treats as a genuine crash)

**Area:** CV / pack generator (`engine/pack_generator/confirm_pack.py` - the one human-confirmation
gate between an AI-suggested pack and the real fill engine; called directly by
`engine/pack/process_pack_jobs.py` on every real SANRAL pack job).

**Scenario:** Finding 138 (2026-11-06) fixed `suggest_pack.years_experience_at()` for a non-string
`initial_graduated` value (a number, bool, or a list/dict - reachable via a hand-edited `profile.json`
fed to this engine's own documented CLI usage) raising `TypeError` from `datetime.date.fromisoformat()`
instead of the `ValueError` its callers already catch. `confirm_pack.py`'s `confirm()` does its OWN,
separate inline parsing of the identical field (`grad = qual.get("initial_graduated"); ... grad_date =
datetime.date.fromisoformat(grad)`, guarded only by `except ValueError`) and was never swept for the
same fix.

Confirmed directly: `datetime.date.fromisoformat(20150305)` (and `True`, a list, a dict, a float) all
raise `TypeError: fromisoformat: argument must be str`, uncaught by this function's own `except
ValueError`. **Worse than just an uncaught crash** - `process_pack_jobs.py`'s own real caller
(`process_job()`) explicitly distinguishes the two exception types: a `ValueError` is "the confirm gate
/ a filler refusing on purpose (the user can act on the message)", recorded as a `"warning"`-severity
system alert with the clean message; anything else is treated as "a crash", recorded as `"error"`
severity with the raw `f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"` text. So this gap didn't just produce a worse error
message - it wrongly escalated a routine, user-fixable bad-data case (go fix the date on the People
page) into what Sarel's own alert triage treats as a genuine bug needing investigation.

**Reachability**: `initial_graduated` is a proper Postgres `date` column (migration `0001`), so the
real, automated `process_pack_jobs.py` path (reading from Supabase) can never actually produce a
non-string value here - same conclusion reached for Findings 141/142 while investigating this exact
bug class elsewhere. The gap is reachable via this module's own documented, standalone CLI usage
(`python3 confirm_pack.py <suggestions> <selections> <profile.json> <out>`) against a hand-edited
`profile.json`, the same vector Finding 138's own writeup names for `suggest_pack.py`'s sibling
`--profile` flag.

**Fixed anyway, by the same precedent Findings 141/142/the original `years_experience_at()` fix
used**: added the identical `isinstance(grad, str)` check, raising the same clean, already-existing
"not a valid YYYY-MM-DD date - fix it on the People page" `ValueError` rather than falling through to
`fromisoformat()`.

**Verified red-then-green.** No dedicated test file existed for `confirm_pack.py` anywhere in the
repo (confirmed by `find`/grep - only `test_form_field_audit.py`, `pack/test_pack_suggestions.py` and
`security/test_tenant_isolation.py` call into it indirectly, none testing this path). New
`engine/pack_generator/test_confirm_pack.py` (first dedicated test file for this module): a minimal,
template-free fixture (`confirm()` against plain JSON/YAML, no LibreOffice/workbook needed) checks 6
non-string shapes (`int`, `True`, `False`, a list, a dict, a `float`) plus the 4 pre-existing, unaffected
cases (a valid date, an unparsable string, a missing date, a future-dated/negative-experience date).
Caught and fixed my own test bug before it ever reflected a real bug: the "future-dated" case first
used a 1-month gap, which rounds to `0` years, not negative - widened to a multi-year gap to actually
exercise the existing negative-experience guard. Reverted `confirm_pack.py` via `git apply -R`, re-ran
- the 5 non-`False` non-string cases failed exactly as predicted (the raw `TypeError`, not caught by
`except ValueError`); `False` was unaffected both times (already caught by the earlier `not grad`
falsy check, same as `None`/`0`/`""` always were). Reapplied - `0 failure(s)`. `py_compile` clean.
Regression: `engine/test_form_field_audit.py`, `engine/pack/test_pack_suggestions.py`,
`engine/pack_generator/test_suggest_pack.py` - all `0 failure(s)`/`ALL PASSED`.

**Regression:** `engine/pack_generator/confirm_pack.py` (`confirm()`, one `isinstance` guard added,
~17 lines including comments); `engine/pack_generator/test_confirm_pack.py` (new file, first dedicated
test coverage for this module). No change to the negative-experience check, the project-dropping
logic, or any other validation in `confirm()`.
