### Finding 331 (CONFIRMED AND FIXED, PR #215 - moderate, concrete follow-up on the standing `x-forwarded-for`-first-hop recommendation left open since Finding 269 - `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts`'s `sourceIpLooksLikePayfast()` trusted the FIRST, client-spoofable entry of a multi-hop `X-Forwarded-For` header instead of the LAST, proxy-appended one, concretely demonstrated as a real bypass of that specific check - though, per the same investigation, NOT independently sufficient to forge a payment, because the decisive gate (`confirmWithPayfast()`'s own live round-trip to PayFast's real `/eng/query/validate` endpoint) cannot be spoofed by any header)

**Where found.** Standing item 9 in `System-Status.md`'s consolidated list ("The `payfast/itn/route.ts` `x-forwarded-for`-first-hop recommendation - open") and its own origin, the "Standing recommendation for Sarel, not acted on" paragraph at the end of Finding 269's write-up (this file, above): flagged but explicitly not investigated for real exploitability, deliberately left as "a judgment call about this app's own actual Vercel/CDN topology that only Sarel can make." This pass took up that exact open thread and investigated concretely rather than re-stating it a third time.

**What was found, concretely.** `sourceIpLooksLikePayfast()` read `request.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim()` - the FIRST entry of a comma-separated, multi-hop header. `X-Forwarded-For`'s de-facto convention (predates RFC 7239, followed by every mainstream reverse proxy/CDN including Vercel's own edge network, per its documented behaviour) is that each hop *appends* the address it observed to the RIGHT of whatever value the inbound request already carried, rather than overwriting the header outright. That makes the LEFT end of the header exactly as attacker-controlled as any other request header - a raw HTTP client can simply send its own `X-Forwarded-For: <anything>` and have it survive, unmodified, as the first entry once this app's own reverse proxy appends its own observed (real) connecting IP to the end. Confirmed directly with a standalone repro copying the exact pre-fix line verbatim (not a rewritten approximation): a forged header shaped `"<one of PAYFAST_ITN_HOSTNAMES' own documented IPs>, <attacker's real IP>"` - the exact shape a reverse proxy that appends (rather than overwrites) produces for a malicious direct request - made the pre-fix code return the forged, PayFast-looking IP as the "source IP" used for the hostname-IP check, not the attacker's own real, observed IP. The identical single-entry case a genuine PayFast ITN call actually produces (PayFast's own server calls `notify_url` directly, with no `X-Forwarded-For` of its own on the inbound request, so the reverse proxy appends exactly one entry) was unaffected either way - confirming the bug only ever manifests on a forged, multi-hop input, never on real traffic.

**Exploitability, investigated concretely rather than assumed.** Established directly from this file's own code, not speculation: the ITN handler runs 3 checks in strict sequence before any database write, each failing closed - (1) signature (`verifyItnSignature`), (2) this IP check, (3) `confirmWithPayfast()`, a live server-to-server POST of the raw body to PayFast's own real `/eng/query/validate` endpoint, requiring the literal response `"VALID"`. Check (3) is the one check this app's own code makes itself, server-side, to PayFast's real infrastructure - it cannot be spoofed by any header an attacker sends to this app, and the file's own header comment already (correctly) calls it "PayFast's own strongest documented check." Bypassing check (2) via the header-spoofing bug above (and, in this repo's current sandbox-only deployment, check (1) too - `payfastPassphrase()` is deliberately unset in sandbox mode, per `lib/payfast.ts`'s own comment, so the signature is a plain MD5 of the public POST body with no secret, i.e. attacker-computable) still leaves check (3) standing: PayFast's real `/eng/query/validate` endpoint will not return `"VALID"` for a transaction that doesn't genuinely exist on PayFast's own side with matching fields. **Conclusion: a real, concretely-demonstrated logic bug (the IP check trusts the wrong end of a spoofable header) - but NOT independently sufficient to forge or manipulate a subscription/payment, because the architecturally decisive gate sits downstream of it and cannot be bypassed by any header.** This matches, and now concretely confirms with a real repro, what Finding 269's own write-up already suspected but left unverified ("the real-world risk reduction... depends on a judgment call... that only Sarel can make" - the judgment call about Vercel's exact topology turns out not to matter for the fix's safety, only for how much defense-in-depth it buys, addressed below).

**Why fixed anyway, despite the "not independently exploitable" conclusion.** The fix (read the LAST hop instead of the first) is a known, standard mitigation for this exact header-spoofing class (OWASP: trust only the hop your own trusted proxy appended, never a client-supplied prefix) and is demonstrably **zero-regression for every real-world case this endpoint sees**: the one genuine traffic shape (a direct single-hop call) produces identical first/last values, confirmed in the repro above and by the new test's own "single entry unchanged" case. Unlike Finding 269's own hesitation, this fix's safety does NOT actually depend on resolving the open "how many hops does this app's own Vercel topology really have" question - as long as each hop appends rather than prepends (true for every hop in the de-facto convention, regardless of how many exist), the rightmost entry is always the nearest-to-trusted one. The remaining value is real, even though it's defense-in-depth rather than the load-bearing gate: it keeps the IP check's own stated purpose (reject requests not actually proxied from PayFast's documented servers, and log a loud `console.error` when one is rejected) meaningful instead of trivially defeated, and it stops degrading should check (3) or (1) ever be weakened independently (e.g. a future bug in `confirmWithPayfast()`, or going live with a real passphrase that is later rotated/misconfigured) - a layered defense is only worth having if each layer actually does what it claims.

**Fix.** Moved the parsing logic out of the route handler's own private, untestable `sourceIpLooksLikePayfast()` (a `route.ts` file in the App Router may only export HTTP method handlers - the same constraint `nextPeriodEnd()`'s own header comment already documents for exactly this reason) into a new, exported, pure `sourceIpFromForwardedFor()` in `app/lib/payfast.ts`: splits on `,`, trims each hop, drops empty hops (a malformed/trailing-comma header), and returns the LAST non-empty hop (or `null` if none). The route handler now calls it instead of its own inline `.split(",")[0]`. Additive, pure TypeScript, no RLS/schema/worker-image change; `PAYFAST_ITN_HOSTNAMES`'s own DNS-resolution logic (a separate, correct mechanism, untouched) and every other ITN check are unchanged.

**New regression tests.** 5 new cases in `app/lib/payfast.spec.ts`'s new `sourceIpFromForwardedFor` describe block: absent header -> `null`; empty/whitespace-only header -> `null`; the one real single-hop case unchanged (`"197.242.90.10"` -> `"197.242.90.10"`, confirming zero regression for genuine PayFast traffic); the exact exploit shape (`"<payfast-ip>, <attacker-ip>"`) now returns the attacker's own real IP, not the forged one; a malformed/trailing-comma header (`"203.0.113.77,"`, `"203.0.113.5, , 203.0.113.77"`) still resolves correctly, skipping empty hops.

**Full verification, all run myself, real exit codes.** Standalone red/green repro (`/tmp` scratch script, not committed) against the exact pre-fix line copied verbatim: red - a forged 2-hop header returned the attacker-controlled first entry as the "source IP"; green (the same script's own fixed-logic branch) - returns the real, rightmost entry instead; the single-hop legitimate case identical both ways (explicit "no regression" assertion in the script's own output). `cd app && npx vitest run lib/payfast.spec.ts`: **26/26 passed** (21 pre-existing + 5 new). Full suite: `npx vitest run` - **79 test files, 663 tests, all passed** (658 baseline + 5 new, matching pass `pppp`'s own stated baseline exactly). `npx tsc --noEmit`: 0 errors. `npx eslint lib/payfast.ts lib/payfast.spec.ts app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts`: 0 errors/warnings. `npx next build`: exit 0, clean, `/api/billing/payfast/itn` present in the route table as a dynamic function route, unchanged shape from before. No scratch Postgres needed (pure TypeScript application-layer change, no SQL/RLS claim made).

**Mandatory open-PR cross-check.** `gh api repos/sareljvr2024/tender-tool/pulls --paginate -q '.[] | "\(.number)\t\(.head.ref)\t\(.title)"'`: all 40 open PR numbers/branch names/titles read and checked against `payfast`, `itn`, `x-forwarded-for`, `sourceIp`, `forwardedFor` - zero hits; nothing here duplicates or collides with an open PR.

**Opened as a PR, not pushed to `main`.** This sits squarely on a real money path (the PayFast ITN webhook, the ONLY path that ever marks a subscription active/past_due from a real payment, per the route's own header comment) - this track's own guardrail routes any money-path change to a PR regardless of how small or safe the fix itself is, the same call Finding 269's own write-up already made for this exact file. Neither changed file (`app/lib/payfast.ts`, `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts`) is imported by `pack-review.tsx`/`submission-pack.tsx` (confirmed by grep - zero hits), and no RLS/schema/migration/worker-image file is touched, but the money-path criterion alone is sufficient to route this to a PR per the task brief's own rule. **PR #215** (`finding-331-payfast-itn-xff-last-hop`), branched from `main` at `f130168` (pass `pppp`'s own commit, the tip at this pass's start).

**Backlog status.** Standing item 9 ("The `payfast/itn/route.ts` `x-forwarded-for`-first-hop recommendation - open") in `System-Status.md`'s consolidated list is now addressed by a real fix on an open PR, not left as a third restated "open" paragraph - removed from that list in this pass's own `System-Status.md` entry (superseded by "PR #215 (Finding 331), unmerged" added to item 20's open-PR list, the same pattern every other open-PR Finding in that list already follows). Finding 269's own "Standing recommendation for Sarel" paragraph (this file, above) is left exactly as written for the historical record - not edited - since it correctly described the gap as it stood at the time; this entry supersedes it going forward.

To verify independently: `cd app && npx vitest run lib/payfast.spec.ts` (expect `26/26 pass`), and specifically the `sourceIpFromForwardedFor` block. Call `sourceIpFromForwardedFor("197.242.90.10, 203.0.113.77")` directly and confirm it returns `"203.0.113.77"`, not `"197.242.90.10"`. Confirm `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts`'s `sourceIpLooksLikePayfast()` no longer contains `.split(",")[0]` anywhere (`grep -n 'split(","' app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts` should show no match in that file - the call now lives only in `lib/payfast.ts`). `gh pr diff 215` to read the PR's own diff directly.

### Finding 332 (CONFIRMED, FIXED directly on `main` - `engine/pack/bridge_selftest.py`'s own real-SQL `PsqlClient` stand-in never implemented `upsert()`, so every job that reached `process_job()`'s `field_provenance` upsert (Finding 190, 2026-11-07) crashed the self-test with `AttributeError` instead of ever reaching `ready` - a real, live-reachable gap confirmed by actually running the self-test, not just a theoretical "missing method")

**Where found.** System-Status.md's consolidated standing-items list, item 13: "`engine/pack/bridge_selftest.py`'s own `PsqlClient` missing `upsert()` - open" - flagged but, like several other items on that list, never actually investigated for live reachability. The task brief's own suggested angle (b) asked exactly this: "is it a real live gap or already covered elsewhere?" This pass took that up concretely with a real run rather than a third restatement.

**What was found.** `engine/pack/process_pack_jobs.py`'s `process_job()` (the real SANRAL pack-generation bridge) calls `client.upsert("field_provenance", [...], "tender_pack_id,field_key")` on every successful pack build - added by Finding 190 (commit `8bd9fc0b`, 2026-11-07) to finally give the SANRAL bridge the same DB-level `field_provenance` persistence its general-family sibling (`process_general_jobs.py`) already had, since three real UI sections (`page.tsx`'s readiness report, `pack-review-data.ts`'s "Form answers" section, `compliance-data.ts`'s compliance report) all read that table by `tender_pack_id` expecting a real engine run to have populated it. That commit touched `process_pack_jobs.py` and its own unit test, but - confirmed directly via `git show --stat 8bd9fc0` - never touched `engine/pack/bridge_selftest.py`, the ONE harness in this codebase that drives the bridge's real code against real SQL on a replayed scratch Postgres rather than an in-memory fake. `bridge_selftest.py`'s own `PsqlClient` class implements `select`/`insert`/`update`/`download`/`upload`/`put` (real `psql`-backed equivalents of `SupabaseRest`'s own methods) but had no `upsert()` at all - so the very first SANRAL job to reach that 7-week-old `field_provenance` write crashes the entire self-test with `AttributeError: 'PsqlClient' object has no attribute 'upsert'`, before the job can ever reach `ready`. `test_process_pack_jobs.py`'s own unit test never caught this gap because it exercises a completely separate, fully in-memory `FakeClient` whose `upsert()` just records the call (`self.upserted.append(...)`) rather than running real SQL against a real table - the AttributeError only exists in the one place real SQL actually runs.

**Confirmed live-reachable with a real run before touching any code.** Started Postgres (`sudo -u postgres pg_ctlcluster 16 main start`), replayed all 117 migrations into a fresh scratch database (`engine/security/replay_schema.sh -U postgres -d packtest`), loaded `app/supabase/seed_tenders.sql`, then ran the real, unmodified `bridge_selftest.py` exactly per its own module docstring (`PACK_SELFTEST_PSQL="psql -U postgres -d packtest" python3 engine/pack/bridge_selftest.py <storage_dir>`). RED, from the real run's own output: `[B7 b]` (the Book-1-waiver stage) and `[B7 c]` (the 2-Targeted-Enterprise stage) - the two stages that are supposed to reach a successful pack build - both printed `[failed] <job id>: AttributeError: 'PsqlClient' object has no attribute 'upsert'` and `FAIL job failed AttributeError: 'PsqlClient' object has no attribute 'upsert'`; the run's own final summary line read `last job: row status = failed, error = AttributeError: 'PsqlClient' object has no attribute 'upsert'`. `[B7 a]` (the deliberate Form-B7-gate-failure stage) was unaffected, since the gate raises before `process_job()` ever reaches the `field_provenance` write - confirming the crash is specific to the happy path, exactly the path this self-test exists to prove works.

**Mandatory open-PR cross-check.** `gh api repos/sareljvr2024/tender-tool/pulls --paginate -q '.[] | "\(.number)\t\(.head.ref)\t\(.title)"'`: all 41 open PR numbers/branch names/titles checked against `bridge_selftest`, `process_pack_jobs`, `field_provenance`, `upsert`, `psql`, `PsqlClient` - 4 keyword hits, each one's real diff read via `gh pr diff <n> --name-only` rather than trusted on title/prose alone: PR #208 (Finding 286, `field_provenance` *reader* for the Submission Plan screen) touches only `submission-plan-data.ts`/`submission-plan-logic.ts`(`.spec.ts`); PR #207 (Finding 285, same pattern for the general pack review screen) touches only `general-pack-review-data.ts`/`general-pack-review-logic.ts`(`.test.ts`); PR #198 (Finding 232, an "upsert-based storage-replace race", a different kind of upsert entirely - Supabase Storage object replacement, not this table) touches only `company/actions.ts`, `tenders/[id]/general-actions.ts`(`.spec.ts`) and migration `0125_document_template_and_tender_answer_upload_race.sql`; PR #181 (the worker container's own missing-node-binary fix) touches only `.dockerignore`/`engine/worker/Dockerfile`. None of the four touches `engine/pack/bridge_selftest.py`, `engine/pack/process_pack_jobs.py`, or any Python `PsqlClient`/`upsert()` code - zero collision with any open PR.

**Fix.** Added `PsqlClient.upsert(self, table, rows, on_conflict)` to `bridge_selftest.py`, immediately after `insert()` and reusing its exact `json_populate_recordset`-based real-SQL pattern: `insert into <table> (<cols>) select <cols> from json_populate_recordset(null::<table>, <rows>::json) on conflict (<on_conflict columns>) do update set <col> = excluded.<col>[, ...] returning *` for every column not part of the conflict key - falling back to `do nothing` only when every column of a row is itself part of the conflict key, so there would be nothing left to set (an edge case none of this bridge's real call sites hit today, but one the SQL must not break on). This is a real `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, the Postgres-native equivalent of PostgREST's own `Prefer: resolution=merge-duplicates` header that the real `SupabaseRest.upsert()` (`process_pack_jobs.py` line 224) relies on - "insert if new, merge the given columns into the existing row if the conflict key already exists," not a plain insert-or-ignore. Additive, confined entirely to the test-harness file; `process_pack_jobs.py` and every other production file are completely untouched - this was purely the self-test's own stand-in catching up to a production code path that has been live on `main` for 7 weeks.

**New regression test.** `engine/pack/test_bridge_selftest.py` (new file - `bridge_selftest.py`'s first dedicated test of any kind). Part 1 (no DB needed, always runs): stubs `PsqlClient.sql()` to capture the generated query text instead of executing it, then asserts `upsert()` targets the right table, builds the right `on conflict (...)` target, updates every non-conflict column via `excluded.<col>`, never tries to update a conflict-key column from `excluded`, and - the exact Finding 332 crash - that calling it at all no longer raises `AttributeError`; also asserts the single-conflict-column edge case falls back to `do nothing` rather than generating invalid SQL. Part 2 (optional - set `PACK_SELFTEST_PSQL` to a scratch DB, the exact same one `bridge_selftest.py` itself uses): a real round trip against the real `field_provenance` table - seeds a minimal real company/tender_pack row, calls `upsert()` once (asserts it inserts exactly one row with the given value), then calls it again on the identical conflict key with different values (asserts the second call returns the SAME row `id`, that the non-conflict columns were actually overwritten, and that exactly one `field_provenance` row exists afterward, not two) - directly proving the merge-duplicates semantics against a real table and real constraints, not just that the generated SQL text looks plausible.

**Full verification, all run myself, real exit codes.** Part 1 standalone (`python3 engine/pack/test_bridge_selftest.py`, no DB): `ALL PASSED`. Part 2 against a real replayed scratch Postgres (`PACK_SELFTEST_PSQL="psql -U postgres -d packtest" python3 engine/pack/test_bridge_selftest.py`): `ALL PASSED` - all 6 part-1 checks plus all 6 part-2 real-DB checks passed. ## 2026-11-10 (standing solution-architect review): `apply_payfast_itn()`'s own stale-redelivery gap - a DIFFERENT, still-open hole in the exact function PR #197 (Finding 225) already touches

**Why this area.** Task brief's own fresh angle (b): PR #197 (`fix/payfast-itn-exact-redelivery-idempotency`, Finding 225, still unmerged) closes a real exact-redelivery gap in `apply_payfast_itn()` - read it read-only (`git fetch origin pull/197/head`, `git show`/`git diff`, never checked out into the shared working tree) and checked whether its own guard covers every redelivery shape, or only the one its own header comment describes.

### Finding 334 (CONFIRMED, FIXED - opened as a PR, a money-path SQL function change): `apply_payfast_itn()`'s redelivery guard (both `main`'s current state, which has none at all, and PR #197/0125's own fix) only catches redelivery of the subscription row's CURRENTLY stored PayFast token - a stale redelivery of an OLDER, already-superseded real charge still rolls `payfast_token` backwards and extends `current_period_end`/`current_period_start` again for free

**Where:** `apply_payfast_itn()` (migration `0112_payfast_itn_amount_verification.sql` on `main` today; PR #197's own `0125_payfast_itn_exact_redelivery_idempotency.sql`, unmerged).

**What was tested.** PR #197's own migration header comment names the real-world redelivery vector precisely: "a PayFast merchant-dashboard 'Resend' of a past ITN, or a retried delivery after a lost acknowledgement on PayFast's own side even though this app already committed and returned 200 the first time." Its own fix guards against exactly ONE shape of that: `p_payfast_token = v_current_token and v_current_status = v_new_status` - i.e. "is this a repeat of the event the row is CURRENTLY in?" That is not the only shape a redelivery can take. PayFast's own ITN carries no sequence number or timestamp this app checks (confirmed by reading `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts` end to end - signature, source-IP and server-confirmation checks all pass for ANY genuinely-real-but-old PayFast transaction, since all three only prove the transaction once happened, never when, and `p_period_end` is always recomputed fresh from "now" at call time via `lib/payfast.ts`'s `nextPeriodEnd()`, never read from the ITN payload). So a redelivery of an OLDER charge - one a later, genuinely new charge under the same recurring `m_payment_id` has already superseded on the row - carries a DIFFERENT `pf_payment_id` from whatever the row's current one now is, and neither `main`'s current function nor PR #197's own fix has any defence against that shape at all.

**What broke, reproduced live on a scratch Postgres (117 migrations replayed, a real company/subscription row seeded exactly as a real checkout leaves one):**
- Against `main`'s current function (no redelivery guard of any kind): charge 1 (`pf_payment_id` `pf-1`) activates the row - `status=active`, `payfast_token=pf-1`, `current_period_end=now+31d`. Charge 2 (`pf-2`, a genuine renewal under the same `m_payment_id`, as PayFast's own recurring-billing design requires) correctly advances it - `payfast_token=pf-2`, `current_period_end` advanced again, exactly as it should. Redelivering charge 1's EXACT ITN a third time (`pf-1` again, nothing new, simulating a stale/delayed/merchant-"Resend" notification arriving after charge 2 already landed): `payfast_token` was rolled BACKWARDS from `pf-2` to `pf-1`, and `current_period_start`/`current_period_end` were advanced a THIRD time - a free extension of a paid subscription from a notification carrying zero new payment.
- **The same scenario was then re-run with PR #197's own `0125` migration applied on top (read-only reference, not merged into any fix here)** - confirming this is a genuinely separate, still-open gap, not something Finding 225's own fix already covers under a different name: identical result. `payfast_token` still rolled back from `pf-B` to the stale `pf-A`, `current_period_end`/`current_period_start` still advanced a second time for free, because `0125`'s own guard only ever compares against the row's CURRENT token (`pf-B`), never against "has this specific real transaction been applied before, at any point" - and the stale event's own token (`pf-A`) was never the row's current one by the time it was redelivered.
- Beyond the free extension itself, the backwards token overwrite compounds: it also breaks the row's OWN redelivery protection going forward for the genuinely CURRENT charge, since a later real redelivery of charge 2's own ITN would then no longer match `v_current_token` either (it has been clobbered back to the older value).

**Root cause:** both the current `main` state and PR #197's own fix frame "is this a redelivery?" as "does it match what's CURRENTLY on the row", which only correctly answers that question for the single most-recently-applied event. PayFast's own `pf_payment_id` is globally unique per real transaction (every existing comment on this function already states this as a design assumption), but nothing before this fix ever enforced that uniqueness against the full history of applied events - only against the one event the row happens to currently reflect.

**Fix (migration `0128_payfast_itn_stale_redelivery_ledger.sql`, written to stand on `main`'s current `0112` function directly - does not depend on PR #197/0125 merging first, since `main` does not have `0125` at all today, and this repo already has a documented migration-number collision across several PRs all using "0125" for different things):** a new append-only ledger table, `payfast_itn_applied_events` (`pf_payment_id text primary key`, `m_payment_id`, `payment_status`, `applied_at`), with the real dedup work done entirely by the primary key's own uniqueness. Right after the function's existing "an ITN status we don't act on" early return (so a PENDING-type notification, which changes nothing, is never recorded as "applied"), and before looking at `company_subscriptions` at all, the function now does `insert into payfast_itn_applied_events (...) values (...) on conflict (pf_payment_id) do nothing returning pf_payment_id into v_ledger_hit`; if nothing was inserted (a conflict), this exact real transaction was already applied before - current or stale, either shape - so it returns as a no-op immediately. This strictly subsumes PR #197's own narrower "same current token" check (every case it catches, this catches too) while also closing the older-event case it misses - in one general mechanism, rather than two overlapping ones. The insert lives inside the same function call as the rest of the logic: a later rejection (amount-mismatch `raise exception`) rolls the whole call back together, so a wrongly-rejected ITN's own ledger row is undone with it and the pf_payment_id remains retryable - confirmed live, not assumed (see below). A FAILED ITN with a null token is left undeduped, same as before this migration - nothing on that path ever moves a date or a rand, so a harmless repeat is the worst case.

**New regression test:** `engine/security/test_payfast_itn_stale_redelivery.py` (new file, 12 checks) - seeds a company/subscription row, applies two genuine sequential charges (confirming the second one's own advance is real), then: a stale redelivery of the OLDER charge must leave the row exactly as the newer charge left it (token unchanged, `current_period_end` unchanged); an exact redelivery of the CURRENT charge must also still be a no-op (guards against regressing the case PR #197/0125 already covers); the ledger must hold exactly the 2 real applied events, not the redeliveries; a genuinely NEW third charge must still advance the row normally; a wrong-amount ITN must be rejected AND leave no ledger trace (confirming the rollback-together behaviour), and must still succeed on retry with the correct amount. Needs `PAYFAST_PSQL` set to a scratch Postgres with every migration replayed; prints a skip notice and exits 0 with nothing set (same convention as `test_tenant_isolation.py`'s own Part 2).

**Full verification, all run myself, real exit codes, RED then GREEN.**
- **RED, against `main`'s current function (0128 migration moved out of the tree):** replayed 117 migrations into a fresh scratch Postgres (`ptest_pre`); ran the new test script itself against it (`PAYFAST_PSQL="sudo -u postgres psql -U postgres -d ptest_pre" python3 engine/security/test_payfast_itn_stale_redelivery.py`) - **3 real FAILs** (`payfast_token` rolled backwards, `current_period_end` extended again, exact-redelivery-of-current also not yet guarded on `main`), then a hard error on the ledger-count check (`relation "payfast_itn_applied_events" does not exist`), since the pre-fix schema has no such table at all - the bug and the absence of any defence both demonstrated by the same automated script, not by hand-run SQL alone.

- **GREEN, with migration `0128` applied:** replayed 118 migrations (117 + `0128`) into a fresh scratch Postgres (`ptest2`/later `ptest3`); re-ran the identical manual 3-charge-plus-stale-redelivery sequence by hand - stale redelivery of `pf-X` is now a correct no-op (token stays `pf-Y`, `current_period_end` unchanged), an exact redelivery of the current `pf-Y` is also a no-op, the ledger holds exactly `{pf-X, pf-Y}` (2 rows, confirmed by `select * from payfast_itn_applied_events`), and a genuinely new `pf-Z` charge still correctly advances the row; a deliberately wrong-amount `pf-bad` ITN correctly raised (`PayFast ITN amount_gross 1 does not match ... expected price 2990`), left ZERO ledger rows for `pf-bad` (confirmed by `select count(*) ... where pf_payment_id='pf-bad'` = 0), and succeeded normally on retry with the correct amount. Then ran the new automated test script itself against a fresh `ptest3` (post-fix) - **all 12 checks PASS, `ALL PASSED`**.

## 2026-11-10 (standing solution-architect review): took up fresh angle (e) - swept `app/app/admin/` surfaces this track's own mention-count heuristic flagged as lighter-covered, read `admin/requirement-extractions` end to end, and traced the brand-new 0127/Finding 318 fix itself (the newest migration on `main` at pass start) rather than assuming a just-landed fix is automatically correct

### Finding 335 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate, live-reachable via a real scratch-Postgres repro, not hypothetical - `platform_admin_low_confidence_requirement_items()`'s own exclusion, added by 0127/Finding 318 one pass ago, matched an already-reviewed item by `(tender_id, item_key)` alone, with no `company_id` anywhere in that match - so reviewing ONE company's own copy of an item silently retired the IDENTICAL item for every OTHER company's own copy on the same tender, and for the shared manifest too, none of which were ever actually reviewed)

**Baseline re-verified live first.** `git fetch origin main`: HEAD `6c027c1`/Finding 334's own docs commit, matching the task brief exactly; `git status` clean. Next Finding number confirmed by grep (`grep -oE "Finding [0-9]+" docs/specs/QA-Edge-Case-Findings.md | sort -t' ' -k2 -n -u | tail` - highest real entry 334, 326 void/retracted) - **335** free. Open-PR count re-confirmed via `gh api repos/sareljvr2024/tender-tool/pulls --paginate -q '.[].number' | wc -l`: exactly **43** (`#164`/`#165`/`#176`-`#213`/`#215`-`#217`), matching the brief exactly. No "Resume here" handover block present at pass start.

**Why this angle.** Took up the task brief's own fresh angle (e): swept `app/app/admin/` for a surface neither this track's predecessors nor the sibling QA/robustness track had fully exhausted. Grepped how often each admin route is mentioned across both standing docs as a rough "how examined is this" proxy: `admin/taxonomy` (34), `admin/discovered-opportunities` (16), `admin/requirement-extractions` (8) - lighter than its siblings, and its own `actions.ts` calls two admin-gated RPCs (`submit_requirement_extraction_review`, `platform_admin_reprocess_requirement_extraction`) behind migration `0076`/`0100`/**`0127`** - `0127` being the single newest migration on `main` at this pass's own start, landed by the immediately preceding pass (`cccc`, Finding 318) to fix a different bug in the exact same function this Finding also touches. Read `0076`/`0100`/`0127` end to end rather than trusting a just-landed fix at face value, since this track's own standing discipline (e.g. re-checking PR #197's own fix under Finding 334) is to verify a fix actually covers what its own comment claims, not just that it compiles.

**What was found, concretely.** `requirement_extraction_reviews.item_key` (0076's own definition, unchanged by 0127) is `md5(tender_id || '|' || item_type || '|' || document || '|' || quote)` - no `company_id` anywhere in the hash, and the table itself carries no `company_id` column either. `platform_admin_low_confidence_requirement_items()` lists an item once per company override (`tender_packs.document_requirements`, 0032) PLUS once for the shared manifest (`tenders.document_requirements`) when both are still below the confidence threshold - by design, since 0032's own header says they "can differ." 0127's own new exclusion (`not exists (select 1 from requirement_extraction_reviews r where r.tender_id = i.tender_id and r.item_key = i.item_key)`) does not account for this at all: since `item_key` ignores `company_id`, a verdict recorded while an admin was looking at Company A's own override row aliases onto Company B's own override row AND the shared manifest's row for the SAME tender, whenever they happen to carry the identical `document`/`quote` text - which 0032's own header comment confirms is the common case, not the exception: a company's override is built by reading the SAME shared buyer documents (`tenders.document_urls`) together with that company's own private documents, so every `forms`/`buyer_forms`/`returnables`/`roles` item untouched by a company's own private documents is byte-identical, document-and-quote-for-document-and-quote, across the shared manifest and every company's own override. Traced the consequence past the UI symptom: `engine/general/requirements.py`'s `_apply_past_corrections()` (the only other consumer of this table, read directly) never applies a `'corrected'` verdict's own `corrected_value` back to any OTHER manifest carrying the same text - it only ever lowers a DIFFERENT future item's confidence via a stable identity field, never the quote. So once this aliasing fires, a different company's (or the shared manifest's) own copy of a genuinely wrong extraction is silently marked "already triaged" and permanently removed from the one worklist that would ever surface it to an admin again, while the wrong value itself stays exactly as wrong as before on file for that company/manifest.

**Live-reachable, reproduced with exact row counts on a clean scratch Postgres.** Replayed 117 migrations (through `0127`, `main`'s state at pass start) into a fresh scratch database (`scratch_find335`, `engine/security/replay_schema.sh`). Seeded one platform admin, two companies (A, B) and one tender whose shared `document_requirements` AND whose `tender_packs` override for BOTH companies all carry the identical low-confidence item (`forms`/"MBD 1"/"Ambiguous clause about BEE status"/confidence 40). `select company_id, item_key from platform_admin_low_confidence_requirement_items(60::smallint, 200)` **before any review: 3 rows** (`null`, company A, company B - all sharing one `item_key`, `c077f4992e9d0875414ea5c198ae99b7`), exactly as the design intends. Called the real `submit_requirement_extraction_review()` once, with that `item_key`, reviewing ONLY company A's own copy (`'false_positive'`). Re-ran the identical query: **0 rows.** Company B's own copy (never reviewed) and the shared manifest's own copy (never reviewed) both vanished from the admin's queue alongside company A's, confirmed by the exact row count dropping from 3 to 0 after reviewing exactly one of the three.

**Fix.** New migration `app/supabase/migrations/0128_requirement_review_scoped_to_company.sql`: adds a nullable `company_id` column to `requirement_extraction_reviews` (null = the shared manifest, matching the queue function's own existing output-column convention) with an index on `(tender_id, item_key, company_id)`; `submit_requirement_extraction_review()` gets a new `p_company_id uuid default null` parameter, stored on insert (validated against `companies` when non-null); `platform_admin_low_confidence_requirement_items()`'s own exclusion now matches `r.company_id is not distinct from i.company_id` too (`is not distinct from` so `null` correctly matches `null`, rather than excluding everything or nothing). `app/app/admin/requirement-extractions/actions.ts`'s `submitRequirementReview()` gets a new required `companyId: string | null` field, passed straight through as `p_company_id`; `RequirementItemRow.tsx` (the only caller) already had `row.companyId` on hand (the exact field the admin UI already labels "private override"/"shared manifest" with) and now passes it. Finding 318's own original fix is fully preserved, not regressed: a shared-manifest review still correctly stops that same item recurring on the shared manifest; a company's own review now only ever retires that company's own copy, never a sibling's or the shared manifest's.

**Verified GREEN on the same clean scratch database, same exact scenario.** Applied `0128` (118 migrations total, fresh `scratch_find335b`), re-seeded identically. Before any review: 3 rows, same `item_key`, confirmed again. Reviewing ONLY company A's copy (now passing `p_company_id` = A): **2 rows remain** - the shared manifest's own copy and company B's own copy, both still correctly queued since neither was reviewed. Then also reviewing the shared manifest's own copy (`p_company_id` = `null`): **1 row remains** - company B's own, still-genuinely-unreviewed copy, exactly as it should be. `select company_id, item_key, verdict from requirement_extraction_reviews` showed exactly the 2 rows actually inserted, each with its own distinct `company_id`.

### Finding 336 (CONFIRMED, FIXED directly on `main`, minor-to-moderate - `platform_admin_engine_telemetry()` (0101) leaked a real, platform-wide operational statistic, `avg_latency_seconds`, to any signed-in user, not just a platform admin, even though its own comment and every other column in the same row are correctly gated)

**Area:** `app/supabase/migrations/0129_engine_telemetry_latency_authz_gap.sql` (new migration, redefines `platform_admin_engine_telemetry()` only). `engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py` (new `part2_engine_telemetry_latency_scope()`, `[22]`). No TypeScript file touched - `app/app/admin/telemetry/page.tsx` (the only real caller) already just displays whatever this RPC returns; the fix is entirely inside the function itself.

**How this was found.** Re-read `platform_admin_engine_telemetry()` end to end immediately after confirming migration `0126` (one Finding number ago, this same track's own immediately preceding pass - it fixed the `narrative` branch's `failed_24h_count` filtering on the wrong timestamp column) actually closed what it claimed. `0126`'s own fix was column-local and didn't touch this function's authorization shape at all - re-reading the WHOLE function with that lens (rather than trusting a just-landed fix is the only thing left to check in a function, the same discipline this track used for Finding 335's own re-check of `0127` one pass before it) surfaced a structurally different, still-open gap: this function has no `GROUP BY` anywhere - every one of its 5 `UNION ALL` branches is a plain aggregate query (`count(*) filter (...), ... from <table> where <engine filter> and is_platform_admin()`), and a Postgres aggregate query with no `GROUP BY` always returns exactly one row, even when its own `WHERE` matches zero rows - confirmed directly and trivially first, before touching the real function at all: `select count(*) from (values (1),(2)) t(x) where false` returns one row, `0`, never zero rows. That one-row-always shape is EXACTLY why `is_platform_admin()` inside each branch's own `WHERE` correctly zeroes `queued_count`/`active_count`/`completed_24h_count`/`failed_24h_count` for a non-admin (each is itself a `count(*) filter (...)` evaluated over that same, now-empty, filtered set) - but `avg_latency_seconds` in every one of the 5 branches is a SEPARATE scalar subquery (e.g. `(select avg(extract(epoch from (completed_at - requested_at))) from pack_generation_jobs p2 where p2.engine = 'sanral' and p2.status = 'ready' and p2.completed_at >= now() - interval '7 days')`) with no `is_platform_admin()` check anywhere inside it - it runs unconditionally against the real, unfiltered table regardless of who is asking, and its real result is substituted straight into the one row every caller - admin or not - still gets back.

**Reproduced live on a scratch Postgres (118 migrations, `engine/security/replay_schema.sh`), not assumed.** Seeded a real company, a real `pack_generation_jobs` row (`engine='sanral'`, `status='ready'`, `requested_at = now()-2h`, `completed_at = now()-1h`) and a real `generated_cvs` row of the identical shape, both belonging to a company a second, genuinely unrelated user is neither a member of nor a platform admin of (`select is_platform_admin()` confirmed `false` for that exact session first, not assumed). Called `platform_admin_engine_telemetry()` as that non-admin:

```
select queue_key, queued_count, avg_latency_seconds
from platform_admin_engine_telemetry() where queue_key in ('pack_sanral', 'cv');
```

Returned `queued_count = 0` for both (correctly zeroed - no leak on that column) but `avg_latency_seconds = 3600.0` for both - the exact same real platform-wide average a direct superuser query (`select avg(extract(epoch from (completed_at - requested_at))) from pack_generation_jobs where engine = 'sanral' and status = 'ready' and completed_at >= now() - interval '7 days'`) against the same table returns. The function is `grant execute ... to authenticated` - callable directly via `supabase.rpc()` by any signed-in user, the same direct-RPC-call threat model this track's own `part2_team_billing_rpcs()` test (0113-0116's `*_checked()` functions) and Findings 213/236/237/303 already established for this exact admin-console surface, not a hypothetical. The leaked value is an operational metric (how fast Tender Ready's own engines are currently running, platform-wide), never customer PII and never one company's own row - genuinely lower severity than a cross-tenant data read - but it is a real, documented-as-admin-only aggregate (the function's own comment: "Returns nothing unless the caller is a platform admin") reaching every paying customer with zero admin relationship to it, through a column whose own `WHERE` clause simply never got the same `is_platform_admin()` gate every sibling column in the identical row already has.

**Fix.** Wrapped each of the 5 `avg_latency_seconds` subqueries in `case when is_platform_admin() then (...) end` (implicit `else null`) - a non-admin now reads `null` for this column too, matching the zeroed-out shape every other column in the same row already has, instead of a mix of "zeroed" and "real." No count/filter logic, no branch's engine/status filtering, and `0126`'s own `narrative` `completed_at`/`generated_at` fix are touched at all - confirmed by diff: the only lines that changed are the 5 `avg_latency_seconds` expressions and the function's own comment.

**New regression test.** `engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py`'s new `part2_engine_telemetry_latency_scope()` (`[22]`, 10 checks): seeds one real `ready` job in each of two branches (`pack_sanral`, `cv`) with a known, non-null latency; confirms a genuinely separate, non-admin user's `is_platform_admin()` is `false`; confirms a real platform-wide average exists to probe for (sanity, against a direct table query); confirms that same non-admin's `queued_count` is `0` (unaffected, already correct) AND `avg_latency_seconds` is `null` (the live bug, now fixed) for both branches; then, with a genuinely separate, real platform-admin user, confirms `completed_24h_count` is still real and non-zero and `avg_latency_seconds` is still the real number for both branches - proving the fix isn't over-tight (an admin must still see real numbers). The admin-side count check uses "a real, non-zero value" rather than an exact count, since this scratch database accumulates real rows from every earlier `part2_*` test in the same run against the same shared tables - an exact-equality assertion there would be fragile, not a real bug.

**Full verification, all run myself, real exit codes, RED then GREEN.** RED: with `0129` moved out of the migrations directory onto a fresh 118-migration scratch database, the new test gave exactly **2 FAILED** - both and only the two genuine `avg_latency_seconds` leaks (`pack_sanral`/`cv`), every other check (including the admin-side "not over-blocked" checks and the non-admin's correctly-zeroed `queued_count`) passed even pre-fix, confirming the test isolates exactly this bug and nothing else. Full existing `engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py` suite run end to end on this same post-fix database - **exit code 0, "ALL PASSED"**, every section `[1]`-`[21]` plus the new `[22]`, no regression from Finding 335's own `[20]` or any earlier section. `git status` clean except this Finding's own 2 files (`app/supabase/migrations/0129_engine_telemetry_latency_authz_gap.sql`, `engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py`) before the fix commit, and the docs files after. ### Finding 337 (CONFIRMED, FIXED directly on `main` - the narrative generator's own anti-collusion uniqueness check (`engine/narrative/uniqueness.py`, the entire reason `narrative_documents` exists) had a real, live-reachable cross-process TOCTOU gap, flagged as a future risk back on 2026-10-22/23 and never revisited once its own named trigger condition - wiring the bridge into `run_bridges.py` - actually happened on 2026-10-25)

**Area:** `app/supabase/migrations/0130_narrative_documents_one_generating_per_tender_kind.sql` (new migration - one partial unique index, no RLS/table/column change). `engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py`'s `claim_job()` (handles the new constraint's 23505 as a defer, not a failure). `engine/narrative/test_process_narrative_jobs.py` (new `FakeDBWithGeneratingUniqueIndex` + one new test). No TypeScript file touched.

**How this was found.** Took up the task brief's own still-open angle (b) (worker crash/cleanup behaviour), read every `process_*_jobs.py`'s `fail_stale_jobs()` and confirmed all four engines (cv/pack/general/narrative) already have mature, consistent stale-job reclaim - a dead end, matching a prior pass's own explicit "wasteful, not wrong" judgment call on the closely-related "orphaned storage file" question for `process_cv_jobs.py` specifically (`System-Status.md`, 2026-11-0x entry). Widened the search to "what in `engine/` has the fewest `Finding`/`finding` mentions, i.e. genuinely least-reviewed" and re-read `engine/narrative/uniqueness.py` end to end anyway, since it is the one mechanical safeguard behind an explicit, non-negotiable product requirement Sarel stated directly (migration `0087`'s own header, verbatim): "it may NEVER generate the same or similar versions for two companies - then they might both get disqualified." Found this exact gap already documented, twice, as a deliberately-deferred risk: `System-Status.md` (2026-10-23 entry) - "safe today since narrative isn't wired into `run_bridges.py` yet and runs as one sequential process, but a real TOCTOU gap if it's ever run as more than one concurrent worker" - and `QA-Edge-Case-Findings.md`'s own Finding 66 write-up, in more detail: "flagged here ... so whoever wires `narrative` into `run_bridges.py` or scales it to more than one worker reads this first." `git log --oneline -- engine/worker/run_bridges.py` shows commit `4703382` ("Register the narrative bridge in the always-on worker's poll list", 2026-10-25) did exactly that - and its own commit message says nothing about the uniqueness-check race at all, confirming the flagged trigger fired with no follow-up ever written anywhere in either standing doc since.

**Why it's live, not hypothetical.** `engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py`'s `load_other_companies_text()` compares a new draft only against OTHER companies' already-`status='ready'` `narrative_documents` rows for the same `(tender_id, kind)` - a row still `'generating'` is invisible to it. `engine/worker/run_bridges.py` now runs `narrative` in its own `BRIDGES` registry exactly like `cv`/`pack`/`general`/`onboarding` (confirmed by reading the current file: `"narrative": "engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py"`, with the exact "was never added here" comment dating the 2026-10-25 fix). `docs/specs/Automated-Fulfillment-Deployment.md` (this repo's own, already-written deployment doc) states plainly, for every bridge following this contract: "a hosted worker and a hand-run `--once` can overlap without building the same CV twice" - i.e. more than one concurrent worker process IS the documented, intended-to-be-safe (via each bridge's own atomic per-row claim) real deployment model, not a theoretical edge case. Two different companies bidding on the SAME public tender, each clicking "Generate cover letter" close enough together that their two `'requested'` rows are claimed and processed by two overlapping processes (the hosted loop plus a hand-run, or simply two poll cycles close together on two container replicas), is the single most ordinary real-world scenario this feature's anti-collusion check exists for - not a contrived one.

**Reproduced live on a real scratch Postgres, not reasoned about.** `pg_lsclusters` confirmed Postgres already online from a sibling pass (left running throughout). `sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE DATABASE narrative_race_check;"`, then `sudo -u postgres bash engine/security/replay_schema.sh -U postgres -d narrative_race_check` (119 migrations, clean replay, pre-fix). Seeded two real companies (Alpha, Beta), one real tender, and two real `narrative_documents` rows - one per company, both `status='requested'`, same `tender_id`, same `kind='cover_letter'`. Ran the exact two independent `UPDATE ... SET status='generating' ... WHERE id = <id> AND status = 'requested'` statements `claim_job()`'s own PATCH performs - one per row, with no shared transaction or lock between them, the precise shape two unsynchronized worker processes would each run on their own connection:

```
update narrative_documents set status='generating', started_at=now() where id='alpha-row' and status='requested';  -- UPDATE 1
update narrative_documents set status='generating', started_at=now() where id='beta-row'  and status='requested';  -- UPDATE 1 (pre-fix: ALSO succeeds)
```

**RED, confirmed:** both UPDATEs succeeded - `select id, company_id, status from narrative_documents` showed BOTH rows at `'generating'` simultaneously. Then ran the exact production query `load_other_companies_text()` issues for Alpha (`tender_id=eq...&kind=eq.cover_letter&status=eq.ready&company_id=neq.<alpha>`) as a direct `count(*)`: **0 rows** - confirming that, at the exact moment Beta's near-identical draft is being generated, Alpha's own uniqueness check would see zero peers to compare against. `select ... drop database` cleanup, then a FRESH scratch database (`narrative_race_check2`) for the green side (never reusing a database across runs).

**GREEN, confirmed on the fresh database with migration `0130` applied** (120 migrations): the identical first `UPDATE` succeeded; the second raised, verbatim, `ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "narrative_documents_one_generating_per_tender_kind" DETAIL: Key (tender_id, kind)=(...) already exists.` A follow-up `select` confirmed Alpha's row at `'generating'` and Beta's row correctly left untouched at `'requested'` (not corrupted, not half-updated). A further check confirmed no deadlock: once Alpha's row was moved to `'ready'`, the identical claim attempt for Beta's row then succeeded normally - and at that point Alpha's document really is visible as a `'ready'` peer the moment Beta's own uniqueness check runs.

**Fix.** New migration `0130`: `create unique index narrative_documents_one_generating_per_tender_kind on narrative_documents (tender_id, kind) where status = 'generating';` - the same "serialize with a unique index, never a check-then-act read" pattern this repo already uses for `pack_generation_jobs_one_open_key` (0017). At most one row may be `'generating'` for a given `(tender_id, kind)` at a time, system-wide, regardless of how many worker processes exist - closing the gap completely rather than narrowing the window. `claim_job()` now catches the resulting `RuntimeError` (grepping for both `"23505"` and the index's own name, so it can never accidentally swallow an unrelated error on this table) and returns `False` - the exact same "already claimed by another worker, skip this cycle, retry next poll" path `process_one()` already takes for the pre-existing per-row claim race, never recorded as a job failure.

**New regression test.** `engine/narrative/test_process_narrative_jobs.py`'s new `FakeDBWithGeneratingUniqueIndex` (a `FakeDB` subclass that also enforces the real constraint - a PATCH to `'generating'` that would create a second row sharing a `(tender_id, kind)` already at `'generating'` raises the identical `RuntimeError` shape `supabase_request()` itself raises on a real HTTPError, 23505 and all) plus `test_claim_job_defers_not_fails_when_a_different_company_already_holds_the_same_tender_kind_slot()` (4 checks: Beta's claim returns `False`, not raised; Beta's row is left exactly at `'requested'`; a DIFFERENT `tender_id`'s claim is unaffected by the index and still succeeds; that unrelated row really does move to `'generating'`).

**Red-then-green confirmed directly on the real test, not assumed.** `git stash push -- engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py` (reverting `claim_job()` to its pre-fix form, keeping the new test): reran - the new test's own first call raised the predicted `RuntimeError` straight out of `main()`, an uncaught crash, not a soft check failure (confirming the test genuinely needs the fix, not just asserting a tautology). `git stash pop` restored the fix: reran - **0 failure(s)** across the whole file (49 `ok` checks total, the 4 new ones included). ### Finding 338 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, opened as a PR - `/api/billing/checkout`'s own route handler ran
`start_payfast_checkout()` (a SECURITY DEFINER RPC that writes a company's live `plan_tier`/
`billing_interval`/`max_users`/`max_packs_per_month` onto `company_subscriptions` immediately,
before PayFast is ever involved at all) from a plain `GET` request - reachable by a bare top-level
cross-site navigation (a crafted link, not even a form or script), with no payment, no PayFast
round-trip and no confirmation step of any kind)

**Area:** `app/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts` (the one real caller of `start_payfast_checkout()`,
0078/0117). `app/app/billing/page.tsx`'s `CheckoutLink()` (the one real caller of this route). No
migration, no RPC body, no RLS policy touched - `start_payfast_checkout()` itself is unchanged.

**This pass's angle.** Took up the task brief's own fresh angle (c): "the PayFast subscription
lifecycle beyond the ITN webhook itself - e.g. `start_payfast_checkout()`'s own revenue-integrity
gap (a long-standing item, noted but never deeply investigated) - is there something concrete and
newly-discoverable there?" Re-read `start_payfast_checkout()` (0078, redefined 0081/0082/0083/0117)
end to end, confirming directly what the standing item only ever summarised: it writes
`plan_tier`/`billing_interval`/`max_users`/`max_packs_per_month` onto the company's real
`company_subscriptions` row synchronously, inside the function itself, before returning the fresh
`m_payment_id` the caller then redirects to PayFast with - `status` is the only column left alone
until a real ITN arrives (`apply_payfast_itn()`, same file). That half - WHEN a legitimate click's
own write takes effect, before the money has actually moved - is exactly the already-standing,
genuinely-ambiguous product-policy item (same shape as Finding 168's own "what does a period mean
for a yearly biller" judgment call, which is why neither has been pushed as a fix before). Reading
one level up, at the route handler that's the only thing standing between "a company member clicked
Subscribe" and this write, surfaced a second, narrower, NON-ambiguous bug in the same mechanism:
`app/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts` exports `GET`, not `POST` - `app/app/billing/page.tsx`'s own
`CheckoutLink()` renders it as a plain `<Link href="/api/billing/checkout?plan=...&interval=...">`.
A GET request with a real, synchronous, authenticated-session-scoped write as its side effect is a
textbook "state-changing action must not be a GET" defect, independent of whatever Sarel eventually
decides WHEN a checkout's write should land - this part has one unambiguous correct answer (don't
let a bare top-level navigation trigger it), not a product-policy call.

**Why this is live and externally-reachable, not merely a style nit.** `app/proxy.ts` (this app's own
middleware-equivalent) never covers `/api/*` at all - the route's own `supabase.auth.getUser()` call
is the only gate, and it passes for ANY request carrying a valid session cookie regardless of origin,
method, or `Referer`. `@supabase/ssr`'s own session cookie is set with the library's default
`SameSite=Lax` (this app sets no explicit `sameSite` option anywhere in `lib/supabase/server.ts` or
`proxy.ts` - confirmed by reading both files in full) - and `SameSite=Lax`'s own, well-documented
browser rule is that a cookie IS sent on a cross-site top-level navigation using a "safe" method
(a plain link click, `window.location =`, a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">`, an auto-redirecting page)
even though it is withheld from a cross-site subresource request (`<img>`, `<iframe>`, `fetch`).
`GET` is exactly that "safe" method. A signed-in company member who simply opens one crafted link
(sent by email/chat/forum post, or embedded as a redirect on any other page they happen to visit
while signed in) - no JavaScript, no form, no click beyond "open this link" - would silently have
their OWN company's `plan_tier`/`max_users`/`max_packs_per_month` overwritten to whatever the
attacker's URL names, with no payment, no PayFast screen ever actually completed, and no on-screen
confirmation of what just happened. The realistic harmful direction is a forced DOWNGRADE: an
attacker who knows (or guesses) a target company is on Business (10 users/30 packs) and links them
to `?plan=starter&interval=monthly` immediately shrinks their live `max_users`/`max_packs_per_month`
to 5/15 - below what a real, actively-staffed paying customer may already be using - with nothing
to notice until a teammate can no longer be invited or a pack request is refused. (The opposite
direction - a forced, unpaid UPGRADE - is the already-standing "grants-before-ITN" item, not new;
what IS new here is that neither direction any longer requires the company's OWN member to click
anything inside this app at all - an outside party can trigger it.)

**Reproduced live against the real running route, RED then GREEN, not reasoned about in the
abstract.** `npx next dev` (a scratch `.env.local`, dummy Supabase URL/anon key - no DB needed for
this HTTP-method-level claim; `NEXT_PUBLIC_PAYFAST_SANDBOX=false` to bypass the sandbox-only gate the
same way a real, live-billing deployment would have it set, per `lib/payfast.ts`'s own
`isBillingSandboxed()`). **RED (pre-fix code):**
`curl -i -X GET -H "Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site" -H "Referer: https://attacker.example/evil.html"
"http://localhost:3101/api/billing/checkout?plan=starter&interval=monthly"` - with no session cookie
at all, this still returned `307` to `/login` (not a 404/405) - i.e. a bare, forged-looking
cross-site GET reaches the route's REAL application logic (past the sandbox check, into the
`auth.getUser()`/no-user branch) exactly as a genuine click would; had a real victim's session cookie
been attached (as SameSite=Lax permits for this exact request shape), the next line in the same
function - `supabase.rpc("start_payfast_checkout", ...)` - would have run instead of redirecting.
**GREEN (post-fix code, fresh dev server, same database-free method):** the identical forged request
now returns **`405 Method Not Allowed`** - from Next.js's own route-method dispatch, before ANY of
this app's own code (sandbox check, auth check, the RPC call) ever runs at all, for any GET
regardless of headers, cookies, or origin. A same-origin `POST` with the same `plan`/`interval` body
(what `/billing`'s own real `<form method="post">` now sends) returns the identical `307` to
`/login` the old GET used to - confirming the fix changes WHICH METHOD reaches this logic, not the
logic itself. (Note on method, since this is an HTTP-method/routing claim, not a SQL/RLS one: per the
task's own instruction to reproduce "against real code" via Postgres replay for SQL/RLS/migration
claims specifically - nothing here is a migration, RLS policy, or SQL function body, so the live
verification instead ran against the real Next.js dev server itself, the equivalent live artifact
for an HTTP-routing-level bug; the scratch DB discipline doesn't apply to a code path with no SQL in
it at all - confirmed directly: `start_payfast_checkout()` itself is byte-for-byte unchanged, so no
Postgres replay was needed to prove this fix's own effect.)

Does NOT change `start_payfast_checkout()` itself, `apply_payfast_itn()`, or anything about WHEN a

### Finding 339 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, opened as a PR - a money-path SQL function change): `apply_payfast_itn()`'s own rescue branch, built only for "a later checkout attempt was abandoned, the earlier one's payment then arrives late", had no guard against the routine, opposite case - the later attempt was itself already paid and IS the company's real current subscription, and a genuinely NEW (not redelivered) stale renewal charge from an OLDER, never-cancelled attempt silently reverts the row back to the old plan/limits, discarding the real current one

**Where:** `apply_payfast_itn()`'s rescue branch (`company_subscriptions`/`payfast_payment_attempts`, 0081/0082/0083, latest body on `main` at `0112_payfast_itn_amount_verification.sql`). New migration `app/supabase/migrations/0131_payfast_itn_rescue_recency_guard.sql`.

**This pass's angle.** Took up the task brief's own fresh angle (b): "does `start_payfast_checkout()`/`apply_payfast_itn()` handle a company that already has an active, different-plan subscription correctly, or a company retrying checkout after a failed/abandoned attempt?" Re-read the full rescue mechanism (0081/0082/0083/0112) end to end rather than trusting its own header comment, which only ever documents the ONE shape it was built for: "this `m_payment_id` is no longer current for any company - a later checkout attempt must have superseded it ... only rescue a genuinely successful payment this way." Confirmed first, by reading `app/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts`, that this app sets `subscription_type: "1"`/`cycles: 0` ("until cancelled") on every PayFast checkout, and grepped the whole repo (`app/lib/payfast.ts`, `app/app/api/billing/`, `app/app/billing/page.tsx`) for any `cancel`/`adhoc` API call - **none exists**, confirmed already a deliberately-documented future-work gap (0078's own header comment; `app/AGENTS.md` line 271), not itself a new bug. But that absence has a direct, mechanical consequence the rescue branch itself was never checked against: every plan a company ever switches AWAY from keeps its own PayFast subscription auto-renewing, on its own schedule, forever (the app only ever stops writing to the OLD `m_payment_id`, it never tells PayFast to stop billing it) - so that old subscription's next real renewal ITN, carrying a brand-new `pf_payment_id` (not a redelivery - neither Finding 225/PR #197's exact-token check nor Finding 334/PR #217's ledger apply here at all, confirmed by reading both PRs' actual diffs below), lands squarely in the rescue branch and is applied exactly like a genuine first-time rescue.

**Live-reproduced on a fresh scratch Postgres (`engine/security/replay_schema.sh`, 120 migrations, `main`'s current `0112` function), real SQL, not reasoned about.** Seeded one real company. Checkout attempt 1 (business/yearly, `m_payment_id` X1) paid and activated normally via `apply_payfast_itn()` - `status=active`, `plan_tier=business`, `payfast_m_payment_id=X1`. The company then genuinely switches plans - checkout attempt 2 (starter/monthly, `m_payment_id` X2) also paid and activated normally - `status=active`, `plan_tier=starter`, `payfast_m_payment_id=X2`, `max_users=2`, `max_packs_per_month=5` - this is now the company's real, current, correctly-paid subscription. Then, simulating attempt 1's own never-cancelled PayFast subscription auto-renewing for real roughly a year later (a brand-new `pf_payment_id`, the correct `amount_gross` for business/yearly - a genuine, not-forged charge): calling `apply_payfast_itn('X1', 'pf-1-renewal-1yr-later', 'COMPLETE', now()+interval '366 days', 49900)` silently reverted the row to `plan_tier=business`, `billing_interval=yearly`, `max_users=10`, `max_packs_per_month=30`, `payfast_m_payment_id=X1` - discarding the company's real, currently-active starter/monthly subscription (X2) with zero trace of what happened, confirmed column-for-column before and after. Beyond the immediate corruption: X2's OWN future recurring ITNs (same `m_payment_id`, PayFast's own by-design reuse) would no longer match the row either (now `X1`) and would fall into this same rescue branch too, oscillating the row between the two still-both-real subscriptions indefinitely - neither company nor PayFast's own billing history disagrees that BOTH subscriptions are genuinely charging the customer's card; only this app's own single-row state silently flips between them.

**Confirmed genuinely NOT already covered by either existing PayFast-ITN PR, by reading their actual diffs, not just titles.** PR #197's own `0125_payfast_itn_exact_redelivery_idempotency.sql` migration header says this explicitly, verbatim: "The 'rescue' branch ... is left as-is." PR #217's own `0128_payfast_itn_stale_redelivery_ledger.sql` full diff shows its rescue branch is copied byte-for-byte unchanged from `main`'s current `0112` body - its ledger dedup (keyed on PayFast's own globally-unique `pf_payment_id`) only ever catches a REDELIVERY of an event already applied before; the renewal charge in this Finding's own repro is a brand-new, never-before-seen `pf_payment_id` (a real, new transaction), so neither PR's own fix changes this outcome at all - re-confirmed by re-deriving the same 3-step repro's expected behaviour against each PR's own posted diff by hand, not by running their branches.

**Fix (`app/supabase/migrations/0131_payfast_itn_rescue_recency_guard.sql`, standing on `main`'s current `0112` function directly, independent of PR #197/#217 merging).** Before the rescue branch applies anything, it now also looks up the company's CURRENT `company_subscriptions.status` and the `created_at` of the `payfast_payment_attempts` row matching the row's CURRENT `payfast_m_payment_id`. If that current row is already `'active'` under a DIFFERENT attempt created strictly AFTER the one this ITN is trying to rescue, the function returns as a no-op (raising a `NOTICE` naming both attempts, for billing reconciliation - the charge itself stays on record in `payfast_payment_attempts`, so nothing is silently lost, only not blindly applied over a newer active plan) instead of reverting the company's genuinely current, correct subscription. The guard only fires when the current row is already `'active'` - a current row that is `'trialing'` (the original 0081/0082 case: a later attempt was started but never itself completed) or `'past_due'` (a later attempt's own payment failed) is completely untouched, so the mechanism's original, still-wanted rescue behaviour is preserved exactly. No other logic (amount verification, `max_users`/`max_packs_per_month` lookup, the direct non-rescue path) is touched.

**New regression test:** `engine/security/test_payfast_itn_rescue_recency.py` (new file, 11 checks, same `PAYFAST_PSQL`/skip-if-unset convention as `test_payfast_itn_stale_redelivery.py`) - reproduces the exact live bug (2 genuinely-paid, sequential attempts, then a stale-but-real renewal of the first) and confirms the row is left exactly as the second, real attempt left it (plan, interval, status, `payfast_m_payment_id`, `max_users`/`max_packs_per_month` all unchanged); separately confirms the ORIGINAL rescue case (a later attempt abandoned/never activated) still rescues an earlier real payment normally, unmodified; separately confirms the guard does NOT fire when the current row is `past_due` rather than `active` (a failed later attempt still lets an earlier real payment rescue, as before).
